articleTitle: Behind Maharashtra drought crisis, sharp regional variation in rainfall
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Maharashtra rainfall deficit Marathwada Vidarbha, Maharashtra soybean yield drop drought 2026, Marathwada crop crisis arhar tur price, El Nino impact Maharashtra rabi sowing, Maharashtra drought, Maharashtra drought crisis, Maharashtra government, Maharashtra monsoon, Maharashtra monsoon season, Maharashtra regional variation in rainfall, Mumbai news, Maharashtra news, Indian express, current affairs
description: Arhar, chana prices are rising, but the real pinch may be felt in the rabi season, if farmers avoid sowing chana and jowar due to the lack of moisture in soil, depleted reserves
body_raw: The Maharashtra government on Saturday declared drought in about three-fourths of the state 265 of its 358 tehsils. The state has recorded a rainfall deficit of 18 this year. But the rainfall over Maharashtra this monsoon season has not been drastically different from other states so far. The country as a whole has a 13 rainfall deficit compared to its 18. Many other states - including Assam and Bihar, which have also experienced floods this season - have much bigger deficits. What may explain the situation in Maharashtra, however, is the large regional variation in rainfall within the state. The worst-hit areas Marathwada and Vidarbha, the two rain-shadow regions of the state which traditionally are drought-prone, have received very little rainfall. Marathwada is particularly affected, having received 38 less rainfall than normal, while Vidarbha has a 27 deficiency. The big deficit is in seven districts - Solapur, Dharashiv, Latur, Hingoli, Jalna, Beed and parts of Nanded, which are away from Godavari river - where rainfall has been just around 50 of normal. Except Solapur, all these districts fall in Marathwada region. Vidarbha region is a little less affected, while western Maharashtra, which is the sugarcane and onion producing zone, is in a relatively comfortable position. Nashik district, known for onion production, has received 37 excess rainfall till now. What happens to crops? Traders and processors say the soyabean crop yield this year is likely to be 40-50 of normal in the Marathwada region, and 60-70 of normal in Vidarbha. The soyabean crop will start arriving in mandis in about 15 days, close to the Navratri festival. Prices in Latur are currently around Rs 5,600-5,700 per quintal, which is close to the governments MSP of Rs 5,705. In terms of availability of soyabean, an expected good yield in Madhya Pradesh is likely to offset the production losses from Maharashtra. The problem is likely to be greater for crops like arhartur pigeon pea, which is a longer-duration crop 160-180 days, versus 80-90 days for soyabean. Arhar will enter the flowering stage around the third week of October and pod-filling would begin around the first week of November. Harvesting generally starts in November-end and continues till the first week of December. Since rainfall is expected to remain sparse under the growing influence of the El Nino phenomenon, which is gaining in strength, this crop could experience terminal moisture stress. Arhar prices are already at Rs 9,000-9,200 per quintal in Latur, well above the MSP of Rs 8,450. The market is clearly sensing a production shortfall. Even chana chickepea prices are at Rs 7,200quintal or so, as against the MSP of Rs 5,875. The real crisis, however, is likely to be experienced during the coming rabi season. The rainfall deficit has left very little moisture in the soil and reservoirs and borewells would also be depleted. Therefore, farmers may not go in for sowing of rabi crops like chana and jowar.

articleTitle: Why has Mumbai’s iconic Gaiety-Galaxy theatre suddenly shut?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mumbai theatre screens
description: Bandra police say the cinema operated without a renewed licence since 2021; management cites burnt cables
body_raw: One of Mumbais most recognisable cinema landmarks, Gaiety-Galaxy in Bandra, has been shut by the police after they found that its entertainment licence had allegedly not been renewed since 2021. The Bandra police have registered a case against the theatre owner, manager and the firm running the cinema under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita BNS, which deals with disobedience of an order issued by a public servant. The police have also pasted a notice outside the cinema directing it to remain closed. A senior IPS officer confirmed the action and said the cinema would be allowed to reopen once its licence is renewed. During an inquiry through the Theatre Branch, we found that the licence had not been renewed since 2021, the officer said. In Mumbai, cinema theatres are required to obtain a Premises Licence from the Commissioner of Police. The licence has to be renewed every year after payment of the prescribed fee and submission of an undertaking confirming compliance with safety requirements, including fire safety norms, police said. The FIR has been registered and the cinema has been closed. If the licence is renewed, it will be allowed to function, the officer said. The closure notice put up by the Bandra police says the cinema has been closed for the next few shows due to non-renewal of its licence. The theatre management, however, has given a different reason for the shutdown. The Indian Express contacted executive director Manoj Desai for his response, but he did not respond to calls or messages. A social media post attributed to Desai said the cinema had been shut because of a technical problem. According to the post, some cables inside the theatre had burnt out and replacement cables had been arranged from Lohar Chawl in south Mumbai. The management said shows would resume once the problem was fixed. Gaiety-Galaxy, which opened in 1972, initially had three screens Gaiety, Galaxy and Gemini. Four more screens Glamour, Gem, Gossip and Grace were later added, giving the complex its popular identity as G7.

articleTitle: Shark Tank India judge richer than Shah Rukh, Amitabh Bachchan, Salman, Hrithik combined

description: Ritesh Agarwal’s Rs 19,900 crore wealth exceeds the combined Rs 19,500 crore attributed to Shah Rukh Khan, Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan and Hrithik Roshan in Hurun India Rich List 2026.
body_raw: Shark Tank India judge and OYO founder Ritesh Agarwal has once again found himself in the spotlight for his business empire. According to the M3M Hurun India Rich List 2026, Ritesh, 32, has an estimated net worth of Rs 19,900 crore, considerably higher than the wealth attributed to Shah Rukh Khan, Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan and Hrithik Roshan in the same list. Ritesh Agarwal among youngest Rich Listers Ritesh Agarwal, 32, is among the youngest Rich Listers featured in the 2026 edition. At 23 and 24, Zepto co-founders Kaivalya Vohra and Aadit Palicha are the youngest entrants on the list, with estimated wealth of Rs 2,600 crore and Rs 3,500 crore, respectively. Ritesh is also among the youngest entrepreneurs to feature in the list. The list, released on Wednesday, lists Shah Rukh Khan as the richest Indian actor with an estimated wealth of Rs 10,000 crore. Amitabh Bachchan follows with Rs 4,000 crore, while Salman Khan and Hrithik Roshan have been listed with wealth of Rs 3,000 crore and Rs 2,500 crore, respectively. Shah Rukhs wealth includes his interests in businesses such as Red Chillies Entertainment and Knight Riders Sports. Ritesh Agarwals wealth vs Bollywoods biggest stars At Rs 19,900 crore, Riteshs estimated wealth is around Rs 9,900 crore higher than Shah Rukh Khans and nearly twice the actors estimated fortune. It is also nearly five times Amitabh Bachchans reported wealth and more than six times that of Salman Khan and nearly eight times that of Hrithik Roshan. Riteshs wealth also exceeds the combined Rs 19,500 crore wealth attributed to Shah Rukh Khan, Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan and Hrithik Roshan in the list. The comparison is notable because Ritesh is not a film star but has become a familiar face to television audiences through Shark Tank India. He was part of the third, fourth and fifth season of the Sony TV reality show, where he appears as one of the judges. ALSO READ The Vvaan movie review Sidharth Malhotra, Tamannaah film is pure torture Hurun Global Rich List 2026 Earlier this year, the OYO founder made headlines after entering the Hurun Global Rich List 2026 as Indias youngest billionaire with an estimated wealth of Rs 18,402 crore. He was ranked 2,816th globally, while Shah Rukh Khan and filmmaker Namit Malhotra, both new entrants to the billionaire club, were placed at 3,306. Hurun also included Ritesh Agarwal among its self-made billionaires aged under 40. The 2026 Hurun Global U40 list said India had eight self-made billionaires in the category, its highest-ever count. The report described him as a 32-year-old OYO entrepreneur who had built one of the worlds largest hospitality companies from Bhubaneswar. How Ritesh Agarwal built OYO at 19 Ritesh Agarwal founded OYO in 2013 at the age of 19. What began as a budget-hotel aggregator has since grown into a hospitality technology company with a presence across hotels, homes and vacation rentals in markets spanning Asia, Europe and the United States. Today, OYOs parent company, PRISM, develops technology products and services for the hospitality industry, with the group serving hundreds of thousands of hotels and homes across more than 35 countries. In an interview with SCREEN ahead of Shark Tank India Season 5, Ritesh recalled that people initially struggled to take him seriously because of his age. He recalled sending cold emails to potential investors without getting responses and eventually finding a major investor in 2015. I was just 18, right out of high school, when I was starting. So, people did not take me seriously at first. They thought a young person was very interested in trying to make a positive difference, but they were not sure if I would be able to do it. Back in the day, when I wrote cold emails, nobody would respond or was not willing to invest. I finally got a big investor in 2015. He also spoke about the first hotel he started with in Gurgaon in June 2013. It had 20 per cent occupancy before OYO came about, but in a few months, the occupancy grew to 80 to 90 per cent. That was the starting point, he said. He added that OYO had since grown to serve more than 17,000 hotels and 1,50,000 homes. Over the years, I have learned that consistency matters. I did not give up, and slowly, more critics started becoming believers, he added. The college decision that shaped his career Riteshs entrepreneurial ambitions came at the expense of a conventional college education. In another conversation with SCREEN, he recalled that when he was 17 and raising his first funding, investors wanted to meet his parents. Their condition, according to Ritesh, was that his parents should agree not to send him to college. They said, if they send you to college, then. they wanted my parents to commit that they wont send me to college, warna unke paise doob jaaenge else they would lose their money, he recalled. He said the investors also told his father, Aap nahi jaante aapka beta itna bright hai You dont know how bright your son is. Ritesh has acknowledged that skipping college was something he sometimes wondered about. In a 2023 post, he wrote that when people asked whether he missed attending college and receiving a formal education, his answer was a resounding YES, while describing the Thiel Fellowship as the adventure that ultimately led to OYO. articleTitle: Drishyam 3 ending explained: Georgekutty’s last move and what Geetha’s final words mean for franchise
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mohanlal starrer Drishyam 3
description: Mohanlal's Georgekutty returns in Drishyam 3 and this time, the threat is not a police investigation or a grieving family. It is thirteen years of accumulated guilt finally catching up with him.
body_raw: For thirteen years across two films, Mohanlals cable operator turned accidental criminal Georgekutty simply stayed one step ahead of the police, of Varuns family, of every threat that came for his own. Drishyam 3, which released in theatres on Thursday, asks a question the earlier films never had to what happens when the man who outthought everyone finally runs out of moves to make against himself? SPOILER ALERT The story so far The 2013 original introduced Georgekutty as a self-educated cable TV operator in rural Kerala. When his elder daughter Anju accidentally kills Varun Prabhakar, the son of IG Geetha Prabhakar, during an assault attempt, Georgekutty builds covers it up so carefully that the police cannot find a crack in it. He creates a false timeline for his family, relocates the body, disposes of Varuns car, and eventually hides the remains beneath a newly constructed police station, reasoning that no investigator would ever think to look there. Drishyam 2, which arrived on Amazon Prime Video in February 2021, picked up exactly where the first film ended. A previously unknown witness surfaces and leads the police back to the station. They dig, and find skeletal remains, resulting in the family arrest for the second time. The climax reveals that Georgekutty had seen this coming years in advance and had already prepared a counter-move. His family walks free once more. The case stays officially unsolved, but the town knows, Varuns parents know, and Georgekutty himself cannot stop knowing what he has done. Also Read Drishyam 3 movie review A close shave for Mohanlal, Jeethu Joseph as Georgekutty battles himself SPOILER ALERT What happens in Drishyam 3 Drishyam 3 is set roughly four and a half years after the second film. Georgekutty has moved into a new chapter of his life. Now a theater owner and film producer, he has made a film loosely drawn from the events that defined his familys life. The movie becomes a hit and in doing so, pulls the spotlight directly back onto him. As both traditional media and social media begin drawing connections between the film and Georgekuttys real past, his mental state starts to crack. He grows increasingly paranoid, unable to read the room he is standing in, unable to distinguish between a genuine threat and his own fear. One night he sees a light moving across his property and finds someone digging in his courtyard. The man doing the digging turns out to be Sahadevan, the constable from the first film who had spent years trying to prove Georgekutty guilty. Dismissed from the police force and now an alcoholic, Sahadevan is still operating, but no longer on his own initiative. Someone is funding him and giving him direction from behind the scenes. That someone is Prabhakar, Varuns father, played by Siddique. Prabhakar has spent years quietly running a conspiracy against the family. He is also responsible for repeatedly sabotaging Anjus marriage prospects. Running through all of this is a thread the earlier films only brushed against, the psychological cost of what the family has been carrying. Geetha Prabhakars mental health has deteriorated visibly. The two families are not enemies locked in a clean thriller narrative. They are people who have been slowly damaged by the same event, from opposite sides of it. Drishyam 3 spends more time sitting inside that damage than any instalment before it. The ending Prabhakar decides Anju must answer for his sons death. Rather than pursue a legal case, he fabricates a fresh crime around her, keeping Georgekutty busy with old legal tangles so he stays blind to what is really being planned. When Georgekutty figures it out, he dismantles the setup from within, rearranging the planted evidence and, in a deeply unsettling move, injuring his own daughter to make her look like the wronged party. But winning has stopped meaning anything to him. He cuts a deal prison for Varuns death, in return for his family never being touched again. Prabhakar gets a warning too, the evidence Georgekutty holds does not disappear with him. Then he surrenders. Also Read Drishyam 3 Movie Review Live Updates Mohanlal-Jeethu Joseph deliver another blockbuster, say fans Rs 50 cr opening day in sight Is there a Drishyam 4? Jeethu Joseph had maintained for months leading up to the release that Drishyam 3 was meant to conclude the story. In multiple interviews, he consistently said a fourth instalment would only happen if the narrative genuinely demanded it, not merely because of box office success. Georgekuttys arrest brings the long-running case to something resembling a conclusion, but the films final moments suggest the familys troubles are far from over. In the closing scene, Prabhakar turns to Geetha and asks whether she is finally at peace. However, she is not. She wants Anju to face consequences for what she did to their son. But the implication is clear enough, the arrest of the father does not close the case against the daughter, and Geethas unfinished grief has just found a new direction to travel in. Whether Georgekutty, from inside a prison cell, can do anything about what is coming for his family is the question the film leaves hanging. If Drishyam 4 happens, that is almost certainly where it begins.

articleTitle: Karnataka job scam: Flat purchased near Bengaluru airport by IAS officer’s kin under lens
articleFeaturedImageAlt: arrested IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar
description: Arrested IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, the then KPSC's controller of examinations, allegedly received around Rs 1.30 crore of the Rs 1.52 crore from candidates as bribes for leaking the entrance examination for veterinary doctors.
body_raw: An apartment purchased in the name of a family member of arrested IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar in Karnataka has come under scrutiny of the Enforcement Directorate in connection with a job recruitment fraud at the Karnataka Public Service Commission KPSC, sources in Karnataka Police said. During interrogation, Basavaraj Kannale, a middleman involved in the fraud, revealed that Gangwar, the then KPSCs controller of examinations, allegedly received around Rs 1.30 crore of the Rs 1.52 crore from candidates as bribes for leaking the entrance examination of veterinary doctors conducted on January 8 and 9. Around 20 candidates allegedly paid Rs 20 lakh to Rs 40 lakh through Kannale, a close associate of Gangwar. Gangwar, 41, served as KPSCs controller of examinations from January 2024 to March 2026. The Criminal Investigation Department CID and the ED arrested Gangwar on August 29 and September 18, respectively. It was found that Gangwar used some of the proceeds of the crime to purchase an apartment in the name of the brother of the IAS officer at the Godrej Royal Woods complex near the Bengaluru International Airport at Devanahalli. The IAS officers brother and family are unaware of the flat purchased in their name in Bengaluru, and they never visited or used the property. It was used by the officer for hosting parties and other activities since it provided privacy, said police sources familiar with the probe. Gangwar has also stated before the ED that a portion of the amount he received from Kannale was used to purchase a flat in the name of his brother, apart from using the funds for buying gold jewellery for his fiance. While the investigations have tracked Rs 52 lakh in bribe amounts being funneled back to the IAS officer - through bank accounts of associates of the middleman - for the purchase of expensive pieces of gold and diamond jewellery at the Bhima Jewellery showroom in Bengaluru for the IAS officers girlfriend, the remaining amount of bribes is untraced. The ED has earlier told the court that the apartment at Devanahalli was bought with proceeds of the crimes at the KPSC. The proceeds of the recruitment frauds at the KPSC were routed through the middleman Kannale and his associates for the purchase of immovable property in the name of his brother, purchase of gold jewellery in the name of his fiance, and payment of personal expenses, a special court for PMLA cases noted last week after an ED submission. The ED has reported that an unexplained amount of Rs 26 lakh was deposited in cash between January 2025 and August 2025 in the bank accounts of a brother and sister-in-law of the IAS officer. The ED is also probing immovable assets acquired by the IAS officer - such as a semi-constructed house in Bareilly in 2025 for Rs 25 lakh, and a real estate construction business launched by his older brothers in 2025 in Uttar Pradesh for possible links to illegal gratifications at the KPSC. Gold jewellery purchases Unlike the property purchases linked to the IAS officer, the CID and ED probes have mapped the flow of Rs 52 lakh of funds from the KPSC veterinary officers recruitment fraud to Kannale and associates, and to Gangwar for jewellery purchases by his fiance. According to the investigations, gold jewellery worth Rs 29.94 lakh was purchased for Gangwars girlfriendin March 2026 at Bhima Jewellery in Bengaluru, and gold jewellery worth Rs 23 lakh was purchased again in July 2026. In both cases, the funds were provided by Kannale. The CID probe has revealed that Rs 15 lakh for the jewellery purchase in March 2026 came from a Kotak Mahindra Bank account of Balu Reddy, an associate of Kannale, and another Rs 15 lakh from the Om Lakshmi Souharda Sahakari Bank in Bidar, operated by Kannales friend Onkar Kamshetti, where aspirants transferred bribes from bank accounts. Gangwar has reportedly told investigators that he asked Kannale to buy the jewellery in July for his fiance through money transfers of Rs 8 lakh from Kannales accountant Umesh and Rs 15 lakh by Onkar Kamshetti, the vice president of the Om Lakshmi Souharda Sahakari Bank in Bidar. Gangwar has made contradictory claims that his fiance issued cheques for repayment of the cost of the gold purchases and that the jewellery purchases were a birthday gift to her. The ED is continuing investigations against the IAS officer to look at whether similar scams were also perpetrated in 12 other KPSC examinations carried out during Gangwars tenure from January 2024 to March 2026. The Karnataka High Court has ordered a SIT probe into two cases of KPSC recruitment frauds, which has been challenged by the Karnataka government in the Supreme Court on the grounds that there were no adverse remarks by the court on the CID probe into the alleged KPSC job frauds. Former KPSC chairman Shivashankarappa Sahukar is also under investigation in the veterinary officers recruitment fraud as well as the recruitment of his daughter through illegal means to the post of an industrial extension officer.

articleTitle: What happened when the lone municipality fire truck went to ‘wash’ a BJP MLA’s house in Gujarat’s Dahod
articleFeaturedImageAlt: dahod MLA
description: The MLA's house is nearly 25 kms from the fire station which has just one fire tender.
body_raw: A BJP MLA allegedly summoning a fire tender from the Devgadh Baria municipality in Dahod district to wash his house has kicked up a controversy, at a time when the states water reserves are under pressure after a deficit monsoon. The MLAs house is nearly 25 kms from the fire station which has just one fire tender. Videos of firemen spraying water on his house in absence of any fire, went viral after which the municipality took a charge from the MLA. BJP leader and President of Devgadh Baria Municipality Dharmesh Kalal confirmed that Khabad had summoned the fire tender for cleaning purpose. He clarified that the cleaning was stopped within 15 seconds as soon as officials informed the fire officer about the deployment. He also added that the municipality recovered Rs 2700 as charges from the MLA after controversy. Sources said, Khabad, a former minister was recuperating in hospital from a major surgery when the truck was summoned allegedly to wash his house in Dhanpur-Pipero area of Devgadhbaria town ahead of Diwali. Most Gujaratis take up deep cleaning of their homes during Diwali, sometimes washing them. However, the timing makes the episode harder to dismiss as Gujarat is dealing with uneven and deficient rainfall, leaving water storage in several reservoirs under pressure. Sources within the BJP say that Khabad, a four-time MLA, who recently underwent a kidney transplant surgery has been advised to observe meticulous hygiene and since he had been away for over two months for treatment, the house was locked and needed cleaning. The incident, however, has made for another awkward moment for the BJP, which has already witnessed a defeat during the recent bypolls of the Municipality following a rebellion against Kalal. eom

articleTitle: Delhi cops had protest under control, then Gandhis walked into All India Radio
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra are detained by police during a protest against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls at Akashvani Bhawan in Delhi on Tuesday. (Express Photo by Gajendra Yadav)
description: Though the Akashvani staff tried to stop them, leading to a tense stand-off, the two eventually made their way inside. “We don’t know what happened.
body_raw: As the INDIA bloc tried to make it to the Election Commission, its leaders ran into police barricades metres from the poll panels office. Soon afterwards, Opposition leaders started getting detained and herded into police buses. The march seemed all but over, and only a handful of Congress leaders remained. Just then, the Gandhi siblings pulled off an impromptu move, upending the script and taking police and their fellow Opposition leaders by surprise. Around 8 pm, police moved in to detain the Gandhis and other Opposition leaders. It all kicked off around noon when Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi climbed a barricade near the NITI Aayog office at Sansad Marg, a few hundred metres from the ECI headquarters of Nirvachan Sadan, and waved the Tricolour as cameras clicked him. Rahul then climbed down as police began detaining MPs sitting on the road. Minutes later, he dashed back towards a bus parked near Akashvani Bhavan, the headquarters of All India Radio, where his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra was seated, catching many Opposition MPs, including some from the Congress, by surprise. As Rahul was about to get into the bus, the siblings locked eyes with each other. Priyanka got down and, along with her brother, walked past policemen towards Akashvani Bhavan, leaving the cops also surprised. Though the Akashvani staff tried to stop them, leading to a tense stand-off, the two eventually made their way inside. We dont know what happened. This was not part of the plan, said a Congress leader. A Congress MP outside Akashvani said, Only the two of them know what they had in mind when they walked in. Congress leaders credited the Gandhis with derailing polices attempts to end the protest. The protest would have been over had they not done this, said a leader. Congress leaders said Rahul made the plan on the fly to use Akashvani as a shortcut to Nirvachan Sadan, which is located near the back gate of the broadcasters headquarters. However, police closed the gate, leaving the Congress leaders to camp on Akashvanis premises. Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel have been stationed outside the Bhavan. While Opposition sources claimed Priyanka was leading negotiations with senior government officials - insisting the protest will continue until they are allowed to meet Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi - the Home Ministry dismissed it as fake. Around 2.30 pm, as reporters pushed their microphones through the grille, Rahul told them from inside the premises, I dont care what the BJP says. Im standing here to protect democracy. What has been done to the country is treason. Be it PM Modi, Amit Shah, the RSS chief, or Gyanesh Kumar, none will be spared. Until reports last came in, Congress leaders led by the siblings were carrying on with the sit-in, with Opposition MPs such as Derek OBrien and Mahua Moitra of the Mamata Banerjee-led All India Trinamool Congress also joining them at the Bhavan. Unmoved. Unfazed. We will not budge until our demands are met. We will not rest until our democracy is saved from the Vote Chors, K C Venugopal posted on X.

articleTitle: Beyond Mughal monuments & ghats: UP putting lesser-known sites on tourism map
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Tulsidas birthplace, Chitrakoot
description: 97 such projects worth Rs 1,425 crore taken up in 35 districts of the state from 2021 to 2026, say officials
body_raw: Uttar Pradesh is increasingly expanding its tourism map beyond established destinations. From the temple town of Bateshwar in Agra district and Munshi Premchands birthplace, Lamhi near Varanasi to the Buddhist sites in Maharajganj and Gorakhgiri Parvat in Mahoba, the state government is turning its attention to lesser-known tourism sites - places with religious, historical, literary, cultural or natural significance but limited presence on the mainstream tourist itineraries. Between 2021 and 2026, at least 97 such projects worth around Rs 1,425 crore were taken up across 35 districts of the state, officials said. The focus is on developing these sites and linking them with existing tourist circuits, rather than concentrating the tourism activity around a handful of established destinations, in an attempt to encourage longer stays and greater local economic activity, they added. They maintained that since Agras tourism identity has long been dominated by its Mughal monuments, Bateshwar offers another aspect - a temple settlement along the Yamuna river which is also associated with the ancestral roots of former prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. The effort is aimed at giving the visitors to Agra another reason to travel beyond the established Mughal circuit and explore a part of the district with a distinct religious and cultural identity. For this, more than Rs 200 crore is being invested in nine projects there, covering the temple complex, heritage conservation, kunds, ghats, lighting and visitor facilities, it is learnt. Varanasi adds literary and Jain heritage In Varanasi, the tourism focus is being extended beyond the Ganga river and major temples. At Lamhi, the ancestral house of Munshi Premchand is being developed as a museum, bringing the citys literary heritage into its tourism circuit. At Chandravati, a project worth more than Rs 17 crore is being developed at the birthplace of the eighth Jain Tirthankar, Chandraprabhu. In Amethi, around Rs 35 crore is being spent to develop the sites associated with Jains, and Guru Gorakhnaths Taposthali and the literary legacy of Malik Mohammad Jayasi. In Chitrakoot, projects at Maharishi Valmiki Ashram in Lalapur, Tulsidass birthplace in Rajapur and Sri Ram Vatika Eco Park near Ganesh Bagh are intended to expand the tourism circuit beyond Ramghat and Kamadgiri. In Prayagraj, Nishadraj Park at Shringverpur is being developed around the traditional association of Lord Ram with Nishadraj. In Maharajganj district, development at Ramgram and Devdah is aimed at bringing attention to sites associated with Buddhism. Officials said such destinations require not only infrastructure but also better interpretation, connectivity and digital information to explain their significance and link them with established Buddhist circuits such as Sarnath, Kushinagar and Shravasti. Chyavan Rishi to Vedic traditions At Gugrapur in Kannauj district, Rs 81.35 lakh Chyavan Rishi Ashram project is being developed around the traditions associated with Sage Chyavan. At Naimisharanya in Sitapur, the Rs 14.09 crore Vedaranyam project will have zones inspired by the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda, along with medicinal planting, yoga, contemplation, music and traditional learning. In Mahoba district, the Gorakhgiri Parvat is being developed around its association with Guru Gorakhnath, while the Sun Temple Interpretation Centre has been planned to bring together heritage, archaeology, yogic traditions and astronomy. A proposed planetarium is expected to add an educational component to the project. In Gorakhpur, two projects worth nearly Rs 47 crore have been taken up at the birthplace of Paramhansa Yogananda, whose writings helped popularise yoga and Indian spirituality internationally. Local suggestions drive development The state is also using local suggestions to identify sites for tourism development. Under the Chief Minister Tourism Development Partnership Scheme, MPs, MLAs, local bodies, trusts, institutions and other eligible participants can propose religious, historical, cultural and natural sites. Projects costing between Rs 25 lakh and Rs 5 crore can receive the Tourism Departments support for up to half of the eligible cost. Tourism and Culture Minister Jaiveer Singh said the states tourism identity should reflect the breadth of its history and traditions. Every district has places closely connected with its people, traditions and history, but many of them remained outside organised tourism because their stories were not presented and essential visitor facilities were missing, Singh said. The expansion of tourism to lesser-known destinations also brings a challenge infrastructure does not automatically create sustained visitor demand. Connectivity, accommodation, trained guides, local businesses, cleanliness, safety and credible interpretation would be important for these destinations to develop as sustainable tourism centres, the officials said. The government is also looking at digital tools to make such places easier to discover. Additional Chief Secretary, Tourism, Culture and Religious Affairs, Amrit Abhijat, said verified digital information, mapping, thematic itineraries, QR-based interpretation and multilingual content could help travellers discover lesser-known destinations. The larger test for the governments plan will be whether visitors coming to established destinations begin adding these lesser-known sites to their itineraries - turning them from individual development projects into functioning tourism circuits.

articleTitle: This is what happens to heart health when you stop GLP-1 medicines
articleFeaturedImageAlt: medicines
description: Stopping GLP-1 medicines does not automatically trigger a heart attack, but some of the health benefits may gradually fade. Here’s what to know.
body_raw: GLP-1 medicines are increasingly used to manage type 2 diabetes and obesity, with some drugs in this class also shown to reduce cardiovascular risk in certain groups. But what happens to the heart when a person stops taking them? According to Dr Parin Sangoi, Consultant Interventional Cardiologist, Wockhardt Hospitals, Mumbai Central, stopping a GLP-1 medicine does not mean a person will immediately have a heart attack. The immediate effects of GLP-1 medicines on blood sugar, appetite, body weight and several cardiovascular risk factors disappear gradually when the medication is stopped, said Dr Sangoi. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. The concern is what happens to the risk factors The issue is not that abruptly stopping the medicine will cause a heart attack, but that the factors it had been helping to control may come back, Dr Sangoi explained. He adds that weight regain, rising blood sugar, rising blood pressure, and deteriorating metabolic health can contribute to higher cardiovascular risk over time. This is particularly relevant for people taking GLP-1 medicines to manage diabetes or obesity, as well as those who already have cardiovascular disease. Do the heart benefits remain after stopping? Studies involving drugs such as semaglutide have demonstrated a decrease in major cardiovascular events while patients were on the treatment, said Dr Sangoi. He explains that the cardiovascular benefits should not be considered to last after the medication is stopped. Studies involving drugs such as semaglutide have demonstrated a decrease in major cardiovascular events while patients were on the treatment. Moreover, evidence suggests that stopping weight-management medications can lead to considerable weight regain and reversal of some cardiometabolic improvements. The degree to which cardiovascular protection continues after stopping differs from person to person, and there is a lack of long-term data that look at protection following discontinuation. In clinical practice, attention should be paid to sustaining the improvements in weight, blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol which reduce cardiovascular risk, Dr Sangoi explains. Should you stop GLP-1 medicines on your own? Dr Sangoi advised against stopping these medicines without discussing it with the prescribing doctor. Stopping a GLP-1 drug should not be something that is done on ones own initiative but rather a decision that is carefully planned, he said. For someone with diabetes, blood sugar may rise again after discontinuation, while people taking the medication for obesity may experience weight regain. For those with existing cardiovascular disease, it is also important to consider why the medicine was prescribed and whether another treatment is needed to manage their risk factors. What if you need to stop because of side effects or cost? Wherever the decision to stop the treatment is based on side effects, cost, plans for pregnancy or some other medical reason, the doctor in charge can determine if the dose should be modified, if another medication should be started, or if more frequent monitoring is needed, Dr Sangoi said. After stopping treatment, regular monitoring of weight, blood pressure, blood sugar and other cardiovascular risk factors can help identify changes early, he adds. articleTitle: Top 10 most expensive houses in the world: Know where Mukesh Ambani’s Antilla stands

description: Buckingham Palace, valued at $4.9 billion, ranks as the most expensive house in the world. Following closely is Antilia in Mumbai, owned by Indian Billionaire Mukesh Ambani valued at $2 billion.
body_raw: Top 10 most expensive houses in the world Owning a home might be a lifelong dream come true for most of us. However, its not the same for high-net-worth individuals HNWIs. HNWIs seek more than just lavish living spaces-the demand for homes that offer unique experiences and cultural richness. In a world where luxury knows no bounds, the ultra-rich around the world have built some of the most opulent residents. Know more about Buckingham Palace in London, UK The royal residence and administrative headquarters of the British monarch in London-Buckingham Palace-is the worlds most expensive house, as of 2024. Built-in the year 1705 and valued at 4,900 million, its architectural beauty and historical significance make it a national treasure, attracting millions of tourists each year. The palace, known for its landscaped gardens, balcony, opulent staterooms, impressive art collection, and lavish ceremonial spaces, is a popular tourist attraction to explore the history and heritage of the British monarchy. articleTitle: ‘Only rate hike or pause ahead’: RBI Governor rules out rate cut in near-term
articleFeaturedImageAlt: rbi governor
description: The MPC’s shift to ‘calibrated tightening’ signals that the RBI is prepared to act if inflationary pressures persist
body_raw: After hiking the repo rate by another 25 basis points bps to 5.50 on Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of Indias RBIs Monetary Policy Committee MPC has sent a hawkish message the era of easy money is far from over, and borrowers should brace themselves for more pain. The MPCs decision to shift its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening is not a mere change in terminology - it is a clear warning that the central bank is prepared to tighten the screws if inflationary pressures refuse to ease. It MPC underscored that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near-term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said after the MPC meeting. With borrowing costs already elevated, another rate hike would pile additional pressure on households, businesses and an economy struggling to sustain momentum. The central banks message leaves little room for complacency. By signalling further tightening, the RBI has effectively chosen to prioritise inflation control over the immediate concerns of growth and credit demand. The outcome could be particularly punishing for consumers and businesses carrying existing debt, as higher interest rates translate into steeper EMIs, costlier working capital and weaker investment. If the MPC follows through on its hawkish stance, the next round of tightening could expose just how much economic pain the RBI is willing to tolerate to bring inflation under control. Malhotra said the duration and extent of the rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses. The MPC observation clearly indicates that another rate hike might be in the offing in the December policy review, depending on the economic conditions, analysts said in initial reactions. Recalibrating policy rate, supply side inflation He further observed that in the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year, with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this financial year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative, Malhotra said. As regards supply side inflation, the MPC noted that monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc., which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose, he said. According to him, it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures in production cost through energy and other inputs as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour. Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist, he said. Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50, he said. Global uncertainty, supply chain disruptions Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty and supply chain disruptions are expected to have some bearing on domestic economic activity, he said. Furthermore, weak southwest monsoon along with strong El Nino conditions may impact the upcoming rabi season and rural demand, he said. The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from the supply side, on account of the deficient Southwest monsoon, El Nino conditions and high volatility in international oil prices. Price pressures are increasingly becoming visible across a range of commodities within the food component, apart from oil, he said. In addition, early signs of inflation becoming generalised are also evident from the increase in core inflation and higher inflation across a larger segment of the CPI basket. Further tightening of global financial conditions, uncertainty about fair valuation of AI stocks, and an elusive resolution of the West Asia conflict pose significant downside risks to the global economic outlook, Malhotra said.

articleTitle: City with Open Hand turns 75: Can Chandigarh grow without losing itself?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: 75 years of chandigarh, chandigarh 75th birthday, chandigarh, chandigarh birthday, Chandigarh growth, Chandigarh turns 75, Indian express news, current affairs
description: Perhaps the bolder question is: Why turn Chandigarh into just another city when India could build more Chandigarhs? The goal should be an India dotted with cities that breathe, walk and shine like Chandigarh, not a Chandigarh that gasps amidst an urban sprawl
body_raw: One of the biggest fears of any Chandigarhian is a city that looks like Gurugram on a very rainy day, or like one of its satellite cities such as Zirakpur cramped, chaotic and stripped of greenery. But Chandigarh has two kinds of Chandigarhians those who were raised here or have worked here for years, and those who arrived here more recently. The former want to retain the standards the city has long offered the latter are grateful that it remains far better than the urban sprawls of most Indian cities. As Chandigarh marks 75 years of its making this October, that difference matters. Its population is at an all-time high, while there is little land left to build upon. The amended Chandigarh Master Plan 2031 has opened the door to vertical growth. But can the city grow upwards without damaging the character of a place built around three cardinal principles sun, space and greenery? And who gets to decide? Residents who have repeatedly gone to court to preserve the citys character? Elected councillors, who can sometimes appear more interested in real-estate development than heritage? Or itinerant bureaucrats who spend two or three years here before moving on? Less said the better about politicians in Punjab and Haryana, whose interest in Chandigarh is often confined to periodically laying their respective claims on it. A city meant to be different The Chandigarh story began in March 1948, when the Punjab government, in consultation with the Centre, earmarked a 114-sq-km site near the Shivalik foothills, as the site for its capital after an aerial survey. It was chosen for its natural drainage, elevated terrain, and accessibility. The city began to take shape in 1951 when the government turned to Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier, who conceived Chandigarh as a living organism. The Capitol Complex was its head, Sector 17 its commercial heart, the Leisure Valley its lungs and the residential sectors its organs. Roads numbered V1 to V7 separated different kinds of traffic. Its spirit was embodied in the Open Hand a symbol of giving and receiving, welcoming everyone. Pierre Jeanneret, Corbusiers cousin, spent 15 years as the citys Chief Architect, utilising local materials and workmen to build its soul. Architect S D Sharma, who worked closely with him and contributed to landmark structures like PGIMER, remains a living link to that era. At a seminar for critiquing the citys planning, the 94-year-old patiently listened before quietly declaring Chandigarh is perfect. It has no flaws. This sentiment has found powerful defenders among the citys denizens. Senior advocate Mac Sarin and other residents fought all the way to the Supreme Court, which delivered a landmark judgment in January 2023 banning the apartmentalisation and floor-wise sale of residential houses in Phase 1, Sectors 1 to 30, to safeguard its heritage character. Citizens also legally challenged a proposed flyover on Dakshin Marg, arguing it violated the citys pedestrian-friendly grid ethos. Lawyers vetoed a proposal to relocate parts of the Punjab and Haryana High Court away from the Capitol Complex. A metro also met the same fate for threatening the citys character. While the Capitol Complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016, Chandigarhs true heritage lies in its green belts, strict sector grids, tree-lined avenues, low-rise skyline, light-filled openness and the Shivaliks. That is what is now under pressure. New faultlines Chandigarh has never been frozen in time. It has grown and changed. The citys industrial belt has new malls, it has built a new underpass, and parts of the high court complex have been modified. Bylaws too are being relaxed. As Bimal Patel, who designed the new Parliament, argued, why should residents not be allowed to make need-based changes in their houses if they do not affect neighbours? Last month, the Administration approved amendments to the Master Plan 2031, allowing high-rises 10 storeys in selected areas, subject to studies on traffic, water, sewerage and ecology. The rationale Chandigarh has only about 114 sq km of developable land. If the city cannot expand outwards, it must grow upwards. Former Chief Architect Sumit Kaur, who helped shape the original Master Plan 2031, disagrees, arguing that drastic changes in one phase risk undermining the idea of Chandigarh as one organism, besides straining its already creaky water, sewage, roads and social amenities. She also underlines the fact that the city falls in Seismic Zone IV. It is strange but we seem to be copying our neighbours instead of the other way round, she says. Architects such as Pallav Mukherjee underline the idea of a pan-regional urban plan and suggest a rethink of transport, with mini-buses running across its vertical and horizontal grids every 10 minutes, to allow for better commute for both locals and those living on the citys outskirts. City Beautiful Chandigarh is not merely an architectural experiment. It is a much loved home, each sector unique. For locals, its truly City Beautiful. Speaking on the legacy of Partap Singh Kairon, the Punjab chief minister who championed Chandigarh, the current Leader of Opposition in the Punjab Assembly, Partap Bajwa, insisted that it is peerless. There is no city like this in the country, he said. BJP national president Nitin Nabin, when asked about the proposed changes to Chandigarh during his visit to Jalandhar a few months ago, also said Its a concept city, it should remain the way it is. Its history is also political. Chandigarh has been the joint capital of Punjab and Haryana as well as a Union Territory UT since 1966. That complicated history is captured by rappers Navdeep Singh and Harsimranjit Singh, who sang Shehar mera Chandigarh. Their ancestral village, Fatehgarh Madran, is now Sector 34. Before Chandigarh was built, this area was the heart of Puadh, they say. Weve always been Chandigarhians. Chandigarh cannot become a museum. It must provide homes, jobs, transport and opportunities for those who have streamed in after its first settlers.But can the city grow without erasing or diluting the very idea that made it different? Perhaps the bolder question is this Why turn Chandigarh into just another city when India could build more Chandigarhs? Seventy-five years from now, the goal should be an India dotted with cities that breathe, walk and shine like Chandigarh, not a Chandigarh that gasps amidst an urban sprawl.

articleTitle: The aloo posto burger is not as innocent as it looks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: now the potato patty sits inside a bun where the rice ought to be. There may be lettuce, perhaps cheese, some sauce or mayonnaise or commercial mustard paste, a toasted surface where there was once steam rising from rice.
description: Fast food will keep borrowing from home kitchens, and home kitchens will keep changing without much ado. For now, the burger can have its moment under the festive lights, and the aloo posto is not going to be displaced from its place with the rice, mustard oil and chillies
body_raw: A cafe chain has put an aloo posto burger on its Durga Puja menu. And a section of Bengalis is incensed - perhaps understandably. The potato mashed, its edges crisped and browned, will presumably be folded into the nutty texture of poppy seed paste, pressed into a patty and tucked into a toasted bun. The umbrage, very likely, is not about the burger itself, but about seeing something intimate, pocket-friendly and comforting being recast in the language of fast food. When a dish has lived in ones home for generations, giving it a new form does risk making innovation feel like intrusion. One of the oft-repeated accounts of eastern Indias culinary history is about how posto became a part of the everyday meal. It is the story of a food born, in part, of the human instinct to make do with what is available. Cultivated in enormous quantities to supply the East India Companys extractive colonial trade, the opium poppy left its tiny white seeds behind for use in local kitchens. Soaked and ground on the shil-nora, the grainy texture of the seeds gives way to a thick, pale paste, almost creamy. The residue of an imperial cash crop was absorbed into the frugal economy of homes. It found a companion in the aloo, a traveller so completely naturalised that its foreignness now seems an affront to the spud. The potato becomes tender and absorbs the posto paste, while mustard oil gives everything a sharp nasal fragrance that softens as it meets the heat of the pan. But now the potato patty sits inside a bun where the rice ought to be. There may be lettuce, perhaps cheese, some sauce or mayonnaise or commercial mustard paste, a toasted surface where there was once steam rising from rice. The ensemble appears to belong to another vocabulary Fast, portable, assembled, engineered for eating with one hand - not licking the fingers. A caveat, however Culinary cultures can become a small place when authenticity becomes a regular test. Posto itself has never been particularly monogamous. There is jhinge posto, with ridge gourd turning soft and almost silky beneath the poppy paste dhyarosh posto, with okra imparting a slippery texture posto with broad beans and other vegetables. There are posto boras, little fritters in which the poppy seed paste crisps around the edges and stays soft within. There are preparations in which posto thickens, coats and binds. Khosha bhaja - salted strips of potato skin embedded with posto and fried until they crackle between the teeth - belongs to a culinary instinct that sees possibility in what might otherwise be thrown away. It is difficult to build a very convincing case for culinary purity in a cuisine that has spent generations finding new things to do with the same small bowl of poppy paste. Is it fair, then, to call the aloo posto in a bun a great culinary transgression? The irritation could have less to do with the burger than with what it seems to say about the food. The faint bitterness of posto rubbing against the starch of the potato, the sharp green chilli, the mustard oil opening up in the heat, the first morsel mixed into rice until everything becomes soft, pale and fragrant - they are memories of meals shared with loved ones. Comfort food has a strange relationship with innovation. We like innovation when it happens to somebody elses food - a paneer makhani or butter chicken pizza, is acceptable to us Indians, Italians balk at the pineapple pizza. We become more cautious when it reaches the foods we recognise by smell before we recognise them by sight. Perhaps that is the paradox that makes the aloo posto burger less innocent than it looks. Home food has never been a museum of fixed objects it has always been about the twists taken by every cook - described with great felicity in the Hindi phrase, haat ka khana - the liberties taken by every generation. But a restaurant changes the transaction. What is unsettling is that the posto whose flavours unfurled bite by bite on the palette is now being announced as an innovation on a festive menu. Dishes are known to wander, and yet they are never quite the prodigal child. Fast food will keep borrowing from home kitchens, and home kitchens will keep changing without much ado. For now, the burger can have its moment under the festive lights and the aloo posto is not going to be displaced from its place with the rice, mustard oil and chillies. I confess I am not averse to tasting the burger. But when the posto meets the aloo, I know I will still reach for the rice. In the years to come, though, the question may well be Will the aloo posto burger be an homage to the East Indian home? Or will it become a marker of that grandiloquent and frequent, but rarely convincing, claim that innovation arrived only yesterday at the chefs kitchen? The writer is senior associate editor, The Indian Express. kaushik.dasguptaexpressindia.com

articleTitle: Flydubai pilot who fought off co-pilot, got stabbed, saved plane was Indian
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar: The Boeing 737 jet, with 174 passengers on board, sounded emergency alerts before landing at the Tabuk airport.
description: Flydubai mid-air terror: Indian pilot Smit Machchhar is being credited with helping save the plane, which landed safely in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk following the cockpit altercation.
body_raw: The Flydubai pilot who was stabbed by his co-pilot on Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday was Indian national Smit Machchhar, who earlier worked with SpiceJet, according to people in the know. According to some Israeli news outlets, who didnt name the pilot and the co-pilot, the latter - identified as an Omani national - attacked and stabbed the Indian captain in what is being reported as a bid to take over the aircrafts controls and crash it. The Indian pilot is being credited with helping save the aircraft, which landed safely in Saudi Arabias Tabuk following the cockpit altercation. He was taken to a hospital in Saudi Arabia after the aircraft landed the condition of his health could not be immediately ascertained. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Saudi Arabia had arrested the co-pilot who apparently tried to crash the plane which had a number of Israeli nationals on board, AP reported. While details about the altercation and sequence of events remained sketchy, some Israeli news outlets reported that the pilot fought back the co-pilot to prevent the aircraft from crashing, with the crew and some passengers then helping in subduing the co-pilot. The aircraft was successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk Airport TUU. All passengers and crew are safe and accounted for, a Flydubai spokesperson said. At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts, the airline spokesperson added. The Boeing 737 jet, with 174 passengers on board, sounded emergency alerts before landing at the Tabuk airport. Before that, it rapidly lost altitude, which likely happened during the altercation in the cockpit. It is not clear yet what weapon was used in the attack, and how the attacker managed to bring it on board. Netanyahu said passengers and crew members on the flight managed to subdue the attacker, preventing a major disaster. I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster, said Netanyahu in his Wednesday statement, according to the AP report. Who is FlyDubai pilot Smit Machchhar Machchhar joined Flydubai in June 2022 as a captain, after serving with SpiceJet for 11 years, according to his LinkedIn profile. He started his flying career with SpiceJet in June 2011, and was a senior commander and line training captain with the Indian airline in Mumbai before moving to Flydubai, an Emirati government-owned airline. With Flydubai, he is based out of Dubai. Machchhars LinkedIn profile lists his flying experience at 9,750 hours. Airline Captain with over 13 years of commercial flying experience on the Boeing 737 fleet, including extensive time as a Line Training Captain. Skilled in mentoring and assessing pilots, with a strong focus on safety, compliance, and operational excellence. Currently a Direct Entry Captain at Flydubai, seeking to contribute further to the training team, his profile reads.

articleTitle: Asian Games hockey: Why the men’s gold tells the tale of triumph and relief
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Gold medallist Indian players, from left, Vivek Sagar Prasad, Manpreet Singh, Yashdeep Siwach, Hardik Singh, Rajinder Singh and Mohith HS during the medal ceremony after the men's final hockey match, at the ongoing 20th Asian Games, in Kakamigahara, Japan, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. (PTI Photo/Atul Yadav) (PTI10_03_2026_000555A) *** Local Caption ***
description: India defended men's hockey gold for the first time in Asian Games' history, but fewer field goals and defence shrinking to shell are worrying
body_raw: As the final hooter blew in Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium, India mens hockey team started celebrating after winning the Asian Games gold defeating Malaysia 5-1. The celebration had mixed hues of triumph and relief. Triumph because the gold medal from last edition was defended and an Olympic berth for 2028 was secured relief because the win salvaged some pride in an otherwise disappointing year. The gold was historic in the sense this is the first time the Indian mens hockey team have defended their gold medal in the Asian Games. Click here to read our Asian Games full coverage In the final against Malaysia, it was a near flawless performance with the Indian forward-line scoring five goals past Malaysia. The 14th-minute field goal from Shello Silverius being the only blip. Skipper Harmanpreet Singh opened the scoring in the 11th minute with his impeccable flick that breached the Malaysian defence but Shello restored the parity in the 14th minute as Indian defence switched off for a moment. Jugraj Singh made it 2-1 in the 23rd minute with another thunderous drag-flick and India went into the halftime with a 2-1 lead. India penetrated deep inside the Malaysian defence multiple times in the third quarter but the only goal came when Hardik Singh wrongfooted goalkeeper Mat Zalmi to score the penalty stroke, which was awarded after a deflection from Mandeep Singh hit the Malaysian defender on the face. The Indian team was relentless in the last quarter with seven penalty corners but India converted only one after Harmanpreet scored in the 57th minute, the last nail in the coffin for the Malaysian hopes. Youngster Shilanand Lakra had already given India a big cushion with a well taken field goal in the 54th minute. There is nothing much to write about the overall campaign apart from the fact that it was the only way for India to mask the disappointment at the World Cup earlier this year and the poor show in the FIH Pro League. At the Asian Games, India was troubled in just one game, which was against Pakistan. The arch-rivals produced a thrilling match after ages. Going into the shell The match just exposed the long-sitting problems in the Indian defence. The Indian defence goes into shell the moment the opposition starts attacking with intensity. Against Pakistan, India were leading 3-0 but went down to 3-3 and constantly lost shape in the fourth quarter before a late strike from Abhishek saved the day. A team that was deemed fittest at one point of time now struggles to catch breath at times in the fourth quarter. It was not the case against Malaysia today, but it is there every time the opposition starts attacking in the last quarter. Coach Craig Fultons mantra is to defend to win. But the team is winning right now but are not able to defend conceding to the likes of Indonesia and Sri Lanka. Field goals paucity If you look at the statistics from the tournament, India scored 58 goals from seven games. The breakup of the goals read 34 field goals, 20 penalty corners, and four penalty strokes. On paper, the stay looks really good but in reality, India scored those 30 field goals against oppositions like Indonesia, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh. Only four field goals came against Pakistan, Malaysia and Japan. India had to rely on penalty corners once a quality defence came up against them. Out of 47 goals against Indonesia, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Korea, India scored overwhelmingly 30 field goals and only 17 penalty corners and strokes. But against Pakistan, Malaysia, and Japan, India scored seven penalty corners and strokes and just four field goals. India needs to find more field goals or more ways to break oppositions defence when things start getting tough instead of relying just on Harmanpreet or Jugraj to score a penalty corner. All is not lost on the team though. With 2028 Olympics qualification done, the Indian team and coach Fulton have a lot of time on their hands to go back to the drawing board and fix things if they want to continue the Olympic medal winning streak at Los Angeles. Nevertheless, the gold had many meanings today, for the Indian team it meant salvaging a poor year overall.

articleTitle: Two captive-bred great Indian bustards released in Rajasthan national park
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rajasthan Minister of Forest, Environment, and Climate Change Sanjay Sharma was also present on the occasion. (Image: @byadavbjp/X)
description: Only about 150 birds of the critically endangered species remain in the wild.
body_raw: Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav and Wildlife Institute of India WII scientists released two male great Indian bustards GIB in Rajasthans Desert National Park on Sunday morning, marking the first step in rewilding captive-bred GIBs raised at two conservation breeding centres at Ramdevra and Sam, Jaisalmer, under Project GIB. The project is being implemented for the long-term recovery of the critically endangered bird. Only about 150 GIBs remain in the wild. Rajasthan Minister of Forest, Environment, and Climate Change Sanjay Sharma was also present on the occasion. In a milestone move, released two male Great Indian Bustards in Sam, Desert National Park, Jaisalmer, today morning. This landmark success has been made possible by the nearly decade-long unwavering dedication of our scientists, researchers and ground staff who have spent years to ensure GIB reclaims the deserts of Rajasthan, Yadav wrote on X. The conservation breeding centres were established to raise a founder population of GIBs that could be rewilded, a measure against the declining wild population. From 2019 onwards, wild-collected eggs were incubated artificially, and chicks were hand-reared. Later, these hand-reared birds mated in captivity. At present, there are 98 such captive-bred birds in these facilities. Around 86 of them are being maintained for captive reproduction, and 11 have been earmarked for release into the wild. Of these 11, two birds were released into the wild at Desert National Park today. Captive reproduction has resulted in 24 live chicks in 2025 and 29 in 2026. Species recovery programme The release of captive-bred GIBs represents the next critical step in the species recovery programme and will provide important scientific learnings for progressively developing and refining protocols for reintroduction of captive-bred birds into their natural habitat, the environment ministry stated in a press release issued Saturday, after the initiation of the rewilding process. Yadav said Saturday that the GIB was important for grassland conservation, land degradation neutrality, and working as an important stopover for migratory birds that travel from the Central Asia flyway. The Central Asian flyway is a large migratory corridor stretching across 30 countries from North to South Asia, connecting the Arctic and Indian Oceans. Besides captive breeding, the project also includes habitat restoration by the Rajasthan forest department, including the establishment of around 200 square kilometres of fenced grassland enclosures inside the Desert National Park. Long-term telemetry studies by WII have identified these enclosures as prime breeding habitats for the species.

articleTitle: DMK gets court permission to sue TVK ministers over Veeramani case remarks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Granite baron R Veeramani faces multiple child sexual abuse cases as Madras High Court clears DMK to sue ministers and TVK IT wing over shielding claims (File Photo)
description: The DMK, which was in power when the allegations first came to light, is seeking Rs 1.01 crore in damages from Ministers Aadhav Arjuna and CTR Nirmal Kumar, and the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam’s IT wing
body_raw: The Madras High Court on Monday granted the DMK permission to pursue a defamation suit against two Tamil Nadu ministers and the ruling TVKs information technology wing over statements allegedly accusing the party of shielding granite businessman R Veeramani, who is facing multiple child sexual abuse cases. The DMK, which was in power when the allegations first came to light, is seeking Rs 1.01 crore in damages from Ministers Aadhav Arjuna and CTR Nirmal Kumar, and the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagams IT wing. It has also sought an order restraining the ministers from making statements it describes as defamatory. Justice K Govindarajan Thilakavadi allowed the partys application for leave to institute the suit. Mondays order concerns permission to bring the proceedings, and it does not decide whether the disputed statements were defamatory or establish the merits of either sides account. The application, argued by senior counsel J Ravindran, sought the courts permission because the TVK IT wings office and the headquarters of social media companies named in the proceedings-X Corp, Meta Platforms and YouTube-were outside the HCs territorial jurisdiction. Filed on behalf of the DMK by its general secretary, Duraimurugan, the suit places the timing of the original police response at the centre of the partys defence. According to the petition, police registered a First Information Report FIR under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act on October 7, 2025, a day after a child rights activist submitted a video clip showing the alleged sexual assault of a minor girl. The DMK argues that this sequence demonstrates that the police acted promptly under its government. The police had in February this year sought to file a closure report in the case, but a POCSO court intervened and ordered a fresh probe. The CMK maintains that the subsequent investigation proceeded according to law and the evidence available, and that it neither interfered in the inquiry nor had any connection or connivance with the accused. Those assertions form part of its case before the court. The DMK also alleges that the ministers remarks were intended to secure political advantage ahead of the Madurantakam and Dharapuram by-elections and to divert attention from what it calls the current governments failures. The ministers opposed the application on procedural grounds. They argued that, because they had been sued in their official capacities as Cabinet members, the DMK should have served notice under Section 801 of the Code of Civil Procedure or obtained permission under Section 802 to dispense with that requirement. At an earlier hearing two weeks ago, the judge had directed the defendants to file a counter-affidavit and listed the matter for Monday.
