articleTitle: AI’s trillion-dollar bet: Will productivity gains arrive in time?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: AI investment is surging as companies pour billions into data centres, chips and other infrastructure, betting on productivity gains that have yet to fully materialise.
description: AI investment is surging to unprecedented levels, but economists warn that the productivity gains and revenues needed to justify the spending remain uncertain.
body_raw: Never has so much cash flowed into a new technology as is pouring into AI, eclipsing the sums splurged on railways or the internet when those technological revolutions sucked in capital. Cumulative spending globally on data centres alone could top 30 trillion by 2050, according to a projection by PwC, almost matching the value of outstanding US Treasuries. It dwarfs what was spent in the railroad or dotcom booms, even after adjusting for inflation, PwC said. Meanwhile, Anthropic, just one of the major firms in the AI race, plans to spend 518 billion in coming years, according to the IPO prospectus seen by Reuters, which is more than 100 times its 2025 revenue. Its backers say AI technology will be more transformational than the advent of steam engines and the industrialisation they powered. Yet lurking behind the dizzying projections and huge outlays by AI companies, alongside sky-high valuations, lie assumptions about vast broad-based productivity gains and future profits with little evidence so far - or historical precedent - to be sure they can deliver, economists say. Productivity gains remain elusive JP Morgan wrote in August that broad-based productivity gains in the US, which leads the AI race, remain elusive, raising questions about the sustainability of AI valuations. A Bain Company study said productivity gains from existing markets would not be enough to justify current outlays and entirely new markets must emerge to close the funding gap, suggesting those could range from using AI-guided robots to developing new materials for batteries and semiconductors. US hyperscalers - the companies rolling out infrastructure around the world like Google, Amazon and Microsoft - and others in the AI race needed to find more than 4.2 trillion of new revenue in the next five years to fund the buildout, Bain said. The question is whether the applications arrive in time to pay for it, according to the study, published last month. Few doubt the potential of AI to transform everything from work in an office to research labs, just as past revolutions shrank journey times from days to hours or connected the world at the touch of a keyboard. What seems more immutable is the maths behind securing a return on investment or the deadlines for repaying loans, leaving economists to work out the implications for the global economy beyond the ups and downs of investment cycles. Historical precedent suggests that technology-driven booms often end when infrastructure buildouts cease to deliver sufficient returns, JP Morgan wrote. Using the example of Nvidia, the US company whose chips are the backbone of the AI revolution, JP Morgan estimated US productivity gains would need to be 3 to 5 annually over the next 10 years to justify its valuation. That would be a substantial increase from the baseline expectation of the US Congressional Budget Office of 1.75 annual productivity growth for that period. For the US alone - which, according to some estimates, accounts for about three-quarters of the global AI investment total - investment will run as high as about 9 trillion from 2025 to 2032, equivalent to spending 3.2 of US GDP each year, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. He estimates the US AI sector would need to generate about 3.55 trillion in annual revenue by 2032 to earn a 10 return on investment. It earns a fraction of that now. The leveraged structure of much of the debt funding AI infrastructure also means a relatively modest deterioration in demand, delays, or asset values can therefore produce much larger losses, he wrote in a conference paper, revised in October. AI and the rate of new wonders The dizzying numbers have not stopped US AI bosses speaking with an otherworldly zeal about changes afoot. Anthropics Dario Amodei has said an AI future could be a thing of transcendent beauty, while OpenAIs Sam Altman has said the rate of new wonders being achieved will be immense as models learn to improve themselves and accelerate breakthroughs. Jasjeet Sekhon, chief strategy officer at Google DeepMind, told a summit at UC Berkeley in August that this self-teaching, known as recursive self-improvement, was a key part of the investment thesis, and that it could, if achieved, deliver unprecedented productivity gains. Recursive self-improvement, while potentially delivering exponential AI advances, has also raised concerns about existential risks to humanity. Yet the pace of change in productivity might still end up lagging the timelines needed by corporate accounts departments. Diane Coyle, an economist at Britains Cambridge University, said the productivity impact of past revolutionary technologies had usually taken about 10 to 50 years to feed through. Anthropics economics team modelled a range of scenarios for how much extra growth AI would deliver at an annual rate in 2030. Assuming a baseline of 2 in a non-AI environment, it suggested growth of 2.4 in a scenario with modest AI impact, 5.4 in a substantial scenario and 15.4 in an extreme scenario. Higher growth would mean more jobs lost, it said, without assigning probabilities for any of the outcomes. Amodei forecast last year that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. For now, however, some researchers say it appears to have been limited to making it harder for those seeking office work to find a job. Studies in the US and Britain have pointed to a slowdown in early career hiring for white-collar positions performing tasks at which AI is adept, even if overall employment remains strong. Researchers at Stanford University said in August that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed industries, such as accountants and paralegals, was 19 lower than for jobs that AI found hard to replicate, like janitors and builders. Yet even if the promised transformation takes longer than numbers surrounding AI companies imply, real economic benefits should stay - just as trains still ran after the Panic of 1873 that bankrupted railroad barons, while the internet didnt shut down after the 1990s dotcom bubble burst. History is our friend in trying to understand this, said Coyle. As long as one is left with the infrastructure thats needed to support all the productivity effects down the road, thats okay.

articleTitle: Riding Elon Musk’s Falcon 9 to space, how a Made-in-Gujarat satellite will help India
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Falcon 9 launches the 18th Transporter rideshare mission and delivers 130 payloads to orbit.
description: Ahmedabad-based space technology startup Satleo Labs has developed India’s first private thermal payload for commercial use. For the next 3 years, data captured will be analysed using AI to generate insights for a range of sectors.
body_raw: Minutes after midnight in India on Thursday, a partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. This was the second of three space launches completed by Elon Musks SpaceX in a 13-hour window on October 1, a remarkable third triple-header from the company in the last two and a half years. Liftoff of Transporter-18 pic.twitter.comVAEHM1NG9K - SpaceX SpaceX October 1, 2026 The first of Thursdays flights transported two American, a Canadian, and a Russian astronaut to the International Space Station on NASAs Crew-13 rotational mission. The second mission, Transporter-18, was a smallsat rideshare mission that put a bit of India and Gujarat into Lower Earth Orbit LEO. Among the 130 payloads on the flight was TAPAS-1, Indias first commercial private thermal-imaging payload, developed by Ahmedabad-based space technology startup Satleo Labs. LEOs can be at altitudes between 160 km and 2,000 km above the surface of the Earth, and TAPAS-1 has been injected into an orbit 500 km high, from where the satellite will capture high-resolution images of heat and temperature variations at locations across the planet. Heres why that matters. What are TAPAS-1 and Satleo? The Thermal Access Platform for Analytics Solutions TAPAS is a thermal infrared camera developed over a period of about 12 months by Satleo, a company founded in Ahmedabad in 2023 by spacetech entrepreneur Shravan Singh Bhati, retired ISRO scientist Dr Ranendu Ghosh, and sales and business development strategist Urmil Bakhai. TAPAS-1 is a CubeSat-category payload, which are a class of cubical nanosatellites that typically measure 10 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm-roughly the size of a Rubiks Cube-and are built using modular units and commercial components that are acquired off the shelf. CubeSats typically weigh between 1.3 kg and 2 kg per unit TAPAS-1 weighs 1.5 kg. According to SpaceX, the 130 payloads on the Transporter-18 rideshare mission included CubeSats, microsats which are small satellites typically weighing between 10 kg and 100 kg and hosted payloads. TAPAS-1 has been designed to capture changes in the heat emitted from the Earths surface in the form of images. This data can be analysed using artificial intelligence AI, Bhati, the CEO of Satleo, told The Indian Express. Of what use is the thermal intelligence captured by TAPAS-1? The use cases span a range of sectors. Thermal imaging data from TAPAS-1 can be used by companies and institutions to gain critical insights into the management of complex issues relating to agriculture and defence, as well as for urban heat management, the monitoring of agricultural and water stress, and detection and monitoring of disasters such as forest fires. Temperature variations across different areas of a city can be tracked in real time. Different areas of a city have different temperatures. This can help municipal corporations undertake the necessary planning to address heat stress, Bhati said. Satleo Labs has already worked with the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation on a pilot project to map temperatures across various areas of the city. Bakhai, the companys Chief Strategy Officer, said the thermal imaging technology can function as a thermometer for the Earth. It can provide highly important data for the agricultural sector. Through this, planning required for crops can be undertaken in a more modern and accurate manner. It can also be useful in urban planning, he said. Besides agriculture, disaster management, and urban planning, Satleo also lists on its website use cases for its thermal imaging solutions in archaeology and geology, which can help detect underground ruins and mineral deposits climate modelling by monitoring of land and ocean surface temperatures and their fluctuations and weather forecasting, storm predictions, extreme weather warnings, and analyses of climate patterns. Does Satleo have any takers for its technology at the moment? TAPAS-1 will remain in orbit for three years, and according to Bhati, the company has thus far received Letters of Intent worth approximately 52 million, of which around 60 have come from companies based outside India. Bakhai pointed out that Most importantly, there is no need to create any large-scale additional infrastructure to use the satellite data for practical use cases. This data will be available directly from the satellite. The company comprises a team of more than 40 professionals, and plans to launch eight more satellites of this type by 2029. Funding of Rs 60 crore has been secured for this planned expansion of operations, the founders said. We plan to launch TAPAS-2 by April-May next year, which will be followed by a more advanced payload PYRO Satleos proposed constellation of 10-15 microsats, Bakhai said. What is the official vision for private companies in Indias space sector? In 2020, the Government of India opened the doors for increased participation by non-government entities in end-to-end activities in the space domain, and followed up these reforms with efforts to provide private stakeholders with regulatory certainty and a level playing field. The Indian Space Policy-2023 was formulated as an overarching framework to implement this reform vision. To develop the spacetech sector and establish the state as a global manufacturing and innovation hub for space technology, the Gujarat government last year notified the Gujarat Spacetech Policy 2025-30, becoming the first state to announce a dedicated policy for the sector. The state government has announced various incentives to startups and private investors in the spacetech sector, including provisions such as assistance for launch costs, support for intellectual property rights, and subsidies for testing facilities.

articleTitle: ‘Clean South Mumbai doesn’t mean clean Mumbai’: Bombay High Court’s reality check for BMC
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mumbai filth bombay high court
description: Blasting the Mumbai civic body over 'filth' in the city, the Bombay High Court remarked that a 'clean South Mumbai doesn't mean entire Mumbai is clean'.
body_raw: Expressing displeasure over inadequate waste management measures across the city, the Bombay High Court on Wednesday pulled up the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation BMC, observing that cleanliness in some parts of South Mumbai did not mean similar steps had been taken across the city. Everywhere there is filth. Only because Worli is clean or South Mumbai is clean, or Nariman Point is clean, that doesnt mean entire Mumbai is clean, a bench of Justices Girish S Kulkarni and Neela K Gokhale orally remarked. The bench was hearing a plea raising concerns about waste disposal at the Kanjurmarg landfill, as well as garbage dumping on city streets and beaches. Once the system is in place and the citizens are also sensitised, one day will come that they will stop doing throwing garbage on streets. And we are looking at Mumbai to be converted into that kind of city where people themselves will go and throw everything in the dustbin. That will happen as we do it when we go abroad, because there are deterrents, there are cameras, but here in Mumbai there is absolutely no worry, Justice Kulkarni said. Even as senior advocate Anil Sakhare, appearing for the BMC, claimed that the situation had improved, the HC said it did not find a very high progress by BMC ward officers in addressing problematic areas related to health and hygiene at public places, hill slopes, pavements and streets. The HC sought a comprehensive affidavit detailing the steps taken by ward officers to ascertain the correct position on the ground, as well as measures taken on Gandhi Jayanti as part of the Swachhata Abhiyan. The judges also said that while travelling to the Maharashtra Judicial Academy in Uttan, Bhayander, they had noticed a plastic-strewn hill near a municipal school in Jogeshwari. Can we believe that this is Mumbai? Simple cleaning will take no more than one day. Nothing has happened. It is unbelievable, Justice Kulkarni said, seeking immediate corrective measures. The bench indicated that it may call ward officers from a few western suburban wards during the hearings, citing a lot of chaos related to waste management in their areas. The judges further indicated that they may soon visit the Kanjurmarg facility for a second round of inspection. The bench will also hear submissions on redressal of complaints regarding odour and environmental pollution from the site at the next hearing on October 22.

articleTitle: World Teachers’ Day 2026: Why October 5 is observed, UNESCO’s 44 million teacher shortage warning
articleFeaturedImageAlt: World Teachers' Day 2026: Why is it observed
description: For 2026, UNESCO has announced the theme “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures.” The focus is on the status of the teaching profession and the challenges teachers face today.
body_raw: World Teachers Day is observed every year on October 5 to recognise the role of teachers in education and draw attention to the professional conditions that shape their work. In 2026, the day marks 60 years of the 1966 ILO-UNESCO recommendation concerning the status of teachers. The date has a specific reason behind it. October 5 commemorates the adoption of the recommendation in 1966 at a special intergovernmental conference convened by UNESCO in cooperation with the International Labour Organisation ILO. The recommendation laid down international standards covering teachers rights and responsibilities, initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. World Teachers Day has been celebrated since 1994. World Teachers Day 2026 This years UNESCO theme For 2026, UNESCO has announced the theme, Standing with teachers 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures. The focus is not only on recognising teachers but on examining whether education systems are giving them the professional and material support needed to do their work. This is also the year in which the 1966 recommendation is being revised. UNESCO says the teaching profession is facing newer pressures linked to digital technologies, climate change, inclusion, migration and displacement. It has also pointed to concerns around teachers autonomy, participation in policy-making, salaries, workloads and working environments. The review is intended to consider how the international framework should respond to these changes. Also Read How this Kargil teacher turned abandoned war bunkers into Social Science labs The issue is particularly relevant amid a global teacher shortage. UNESCO says 44 million additional teachers will be needed by 2030 to achieve universal primary and secondary education. The figure covers the scale of the global recruitment challenge and places teacher supply alongside questions of retention and working conditions. The global 2026 World Teachers Day celebration will be held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris on October 5. Teachers, ministers and other education stakeholders are expected to participate in discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the profession. Also Read He once saw education as his only way to a job. Now, hes a national award-winning teacher The programme will also include the award ceremony for the ninth UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development. World Teachers Day, therefore, is both a recognition of teachers and a day centred on the standards, rights and conditions that underpin the teaching profession.

articleTitle: West Bengal announces Rs 50,000 study grant for women

Also Read Karnataka plans AI training in government schools from Class 6 In his statement to reporters at the state secretariat after a Cabinet meeting, Adhikari said that the State Public Service Commission and the State Police Recruitment Board would carry out the examination and recruitment process for the newly approved vacancies. We had promised to provide one lakh government jobs in the state, and we are moving towards that goal. The PSC is now working at full strength to complete all pending recruitment processes, he added. The announced vacancies will be filled across various state departments, including forests, fire services, prisons, home and hill affairs, he said. On the police recruitment, Adhikari said appointment-related formalities for around 12,000 posts would be conducted on October 11, and about 5,000 shortlisted candidates would receive their appointment letters at a programme on the same day. articleTitle: World News Updates: Two bodies recovered from site of avalanche at Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal
articleFeaturedImageAlt: A view of damaged structure following the flash flood in Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on September 1, 2026. (Express Photo by Tashi Tobgyal)
description: Rescue teams search for 14 people missing after avalanche in Nepal’s Manang district.
body_raw: At least two bodies were recovered on Sunday after an avalanche hit the Himlung Himal area of Manang in Nepal. The identification of the two bodies is yet to be carried out. The Kathmandu Post reported that another 14 people remain missing in the incident. Meanwhile, Irans Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps IRGC Navy said on Sunday that it has seized a US Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle operating in the Strait of Hormuz , which it said was conducting espionage, Reuters reported, quoting state media. The IRGC said the vehicle had been captured using intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities and was being examined by Iranian specialists to recover its data. Meanwhile, at least 27 people were killed and 26 wounded in two separate mass shootings in South African townships within a few hours, police said. The first shooting took place at a bar in Wedela township near Johannesburg, where eight gunmen allegedly opened fire, killing 17 people and injuring 15 others. About four hours later, 10 people were killed and 11 wounded in a shooting at a store in Lwandle township near Cape Town. No arrests had been made in either case, while police were searching for the suspects. Suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols, the statement said of the shooting, which occurred around 930 p.m. 1930 GMT on Saturday in Gauteng province. Meanwhile, The United States has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt fighting in the region, President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday, prompting Tehran to reiterate on Sunday that only diplomatic negotiation can resolve the conflict. The initiative had been floated earlier in the week at the UN General Assembly in New York, where Iran described it as a seven-day roadmap transmitted to Washington through Qatari mediators that would end hostilities and reopen the critical waterway. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehrans conditions remain unmet and that Iran is still awaiting a definitive response through the mediators before deciding its next move. Trump I reject their proposal. I rejected their deal Speaking to reporters at the White House on Saturday, Trump said he had turned down the Iranian offer, framing it as a sign of Tehrans weakness rather than genuine goodwill. He argued Iran is pushing for an agreement because economic pressure is mounting on the regime, telling reporters the country wants to make a deal because its losing badly and running out of money. Key world developments Mediators havent confirmed rejection Despite Trumps public comments, Araghchi said mediators have not yet officially conveyed a US rejection of the plan, and Iran will act once it receives their definitive views. Seven-day ceasefire framework Araghchi said the proposal, if accepted, would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the Strait of Hormuz alongside a pause in regional fighting, with wider talks to follow on mutually agreed subjects. Nuclear program off the table A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran would show no flexibility on its nuclear program including uranium enrichment even if Washington accepted the broader peace deal. Pezeshkians dual message Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on CBSs Face the Nation that Tehran is open to talks but wont accept bullying or coercion, while separately telling Al Jazeera that Qatar and Pakistan are relaying Irans messages to Washington. articleTitle: Sujeet Kalkal wants the mat, not the functions, before the World Championships
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Sujeet
description: The Asian Games champion, who has won 19 bouts in a row, says the ground game is what he must fix before Kazakhstan
body_raw: Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal has had a great week. He brought the mens 65 kg freestyle gold home from the Asian Games after defeating Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka of Japan in the semi-final and winning the final from 2-9 down. He also won the Raja Randhir Singh award for the best Indian male athlete at the Asian Games 2026. However, the 23-year-old from Charkhi Dadri doesnt want to lose himself in the celebrations right now.After winning the Asian Games medal, there are some distractions like functions and everything. But I want to go back to the mat as soon as possible, Sujeet said at an interaction organised by SAI Media. He is right to want to get back to the mat a tough World Championships awaits him in Kazakhstan, starting October 24. Sujeet is on a dominant run in the mens 65 kg category. He is the reigning U23 World Champion, Asian champion and Asian Games gold medallist. Since losing the bronze-medal match at last years World Championships, Sujeet has won 19 bouts in a row and is unbeaten at the national level too. The World Championships will bring new challenges the Iranian powerhouse Rahman Amouzadkhalili, to whom Sujeet lost last year, and the American prodigy Bowen Bassett, who beat Worlds bronze medallist Real Marshall Ray Woods in the US trials. The competition level in the World Championships is very tough and it is not going to be easy for me. It is certainly more competitive than the Asian Games and that is what makes it more exciting. This is the most important competition for me, Sujeet said. But he has a few things to fine-tune before he goes for a world title. I need to learn from the mistakes that I made in the past competitions. So, I am going to focus on that, he said. Sujeets Asian Games campaign was near flawless, but he gave away easy points at the start of bouts, especially in positions played out on the mat. One of the reasons that Sujeet trailed in the final was that he gave a more advantageous position to the opponent on the ground. That is something we are going to work on in this small time frame we have got, his coach Kuldeep Singh told The Indian Express. Sujeet agrees. Both my coaches Kuldeep and Shako have asked me to take a strong position on the ground. I am working on it. Right now, I need to attack on the ground well and also defend if I lose the attacking position, he explained. The other thing he has to do more of is attack, something national coach Bentinidis Shako also insists on. Before the Asian Games, I had played a tournament in Russia. I won that tournament and every bout in it. But coach Shako was not happy with it, Sujeet said. He told me to attack more as I have a variety of attacks. He did that at the Asian Games, but will need to do more of it at the World Championships. I worked on it and executed it during the Asian Games. That is why I was able to score so many points. I think I will need to continue doing this at the World Championships, said Sujeet. Shako, who also coached Bajrang Punia to an Olympic medal, has brought attacking changes to Sujeets game. One of the highlights of Sujeets Asian Games campaign was his use of the dhobi pachad in the bout against the Iranian wrestler. It is a classic Indian kushti technique that uses the opponents momentum and a tight upper-body grip to lift and arc them over the shoulder or back. I have to thank coach Shako for that. I used to try the technique in practice but never really executed it on the mat. But coach Shako made some corrections to it. He asked me to practice it over and over. I think I executed it because of the regular practice of the move, said Sujeet. Sujeet has less than 15 days to finish with the functions, work on his ground wrestling and head to Astana, Kazakhstan, where he could become only the second Indian to win a wrestling world title.

articleTitle: Gen Z reacts to Aashiqui: Rahul Roy-Anu Aggarwal film feels more dated than entertaining
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Gen Z reacts to Mahesh Bhatt's Aashiqui
description: On Mahesh Bhatt's birthday, I, a Gen Z viewer, watched his 1990 romantic drama Aashiqui, which marked the debut of Rahul Roy and Anu Aggarwal.
body_raw: Mahesh Bhatts 1990 musical romance Aashiqui was a cultural phenomenon that turned debutants Rahul Roy and Anu Aggarwal into overnight stars. But watching the blockbuster for the first time 36 years later, on Maheshs birthday, I struggled to understand the hype as a Gen Z viewer. Barely 10 minutes into the film, I found myself wondering Why did people go wild over this movie? The Aashiqui 2 comparison I was already familiar with the Aashiqui template, having watched Aditya Roy Kapur and Shraddha Kapoors Aashiqui 2 2013, directed by Mohit Suri. The romantic musical was a commercial success, and for good reason. But watching Aashiqui for the first time, I was surprised by how different the two films felt, largely because of the eras they were made in. As a Gen Z viewer, there is something almost alien about watching a love story in which nobody is constantly reachable. The 1990 film felt slow to me, and I often grew restless watching it. The difference became even more apparent in Rahul Roy and Anu Aggarwals performances, which can feel a little stiff by todays standards. But perhaps thats also what makes the comparison interesting Aditya and Shraddha could run in Aashiqui 2 because Rahul and Anu had already walked in Aashiqui. Romance has aged differently You know youre watching a 90s film when an electricity bill becomes a means of communication between two lovers. And after writing his message on the bill, Rahul needs to get it back - otherwise, his house could literally be plunged into darkness because of non-payment. Today, texting has made communication almost instant. Back then, you simply had to wait. Through my Gen Z lens, that waiting often made the romance feel slow and, at times, boring. ALSO READ Paid grocer Rs 1 per message Mushtaq Khan reveals unusual way he got Mahesh Bhatts call There were several such supposedly classic romantic moments that I struggled to relate to as a viewer. This simply isnt how my generation experiences or defines romance. What did work for me, however, was the way the songs were woven into the love story. T The problematic opening sequence The most alarming part of Mahesh Bhatts Aashiqui, for me, was its opening sequence, when Rahul first sees Anu at a police station. After Anu runs away from her hostel, how does a police officer simply allow the hostel warden to take her back despite her resistance? What about her consent? As a Gen Z viewer, these are questions that are difficult to ignore in 2026. If Aashiqui were released today, the scene would likely spark reels, Reddit threads and endless social media debates about what the film was showing and normalising. Would Aashiqui work today? Special mention The late Reema Lagoo looked beautiful in Aashiqui. My strongest memory of her is from Sooraj Barjatyas Hum Saath-Saath Hain, so watching her here felt like discovering an actor I had only known from a later phase of her career. Having said that, as a Gen Z viewer, I dont think Mahesh Bhatts Aashiqui would work in 2026 the way it did in 1990. The emotions that the romantic musical wanted me to feel simply didnt land the way they perhaps did for audiences back then. Thirty-six years later, the Rahul Roy and Anu Aggarwal-starrer felt more dated than entertaining to me.

articleTitle: Sexual misconduct complaint: Hockey umpire from India sent back, he rejects charge
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hockey
description: A Malaysian female official complained about inappropriate touch and non-consensual physical contact
body_raw: An international hockey umpire from India, Gurinder Singh Sangha, has been sent back from the Asian Games in Japan following allegations of sexual misconduct. He has rejected the allegations and denied any wrongdoing. Sources said Sangha was asked to leave Nagoya Wednesday after a woman umpire from Malaysia accused him of inappropriate touch and non-consensual physical contact on the pretext of mentoring her. Sangha, the sources said, also faces allegations of misbehaviour with a woman staff member at the hotel where he stayed for the Asian Games after allegedly calling her to his room. Hockey India secretary general Bholanath Singh, who is in Nagoya, was not available for comment. The Asian Hockey Federation did not respond to an email seeking comment. A senior official from Hockey India said, He Sangha was sent back two days ago after the Malaysian umpire complained. We will take action if the Asian Hockey Federation gives us a detailed report. Sangha, meanwhile, denied the allegations, calling it an attempt at character assassination. Reached for comment, he said, I totally deny these allegations. Everyone in the hockey world knows me. Its a character assassination. I only got to know about this from the media. There have been some administrative issues with higher authorities and I had made my mind up to retire after the Asian Games. Sangha, who became an international hockey umpire in 2003 and was inducted into the umpire managers panel in 2017, claimed he didnt have any interaction with women officials during his stay at the Asian Games, and his premature return home was due to family issues. I have been handling mens umpire panels and there is no association with any female umpire or any other female. Such allegations are a result of vendetta against officials like me. The environment in hockey is getting worse day by day, he said. My flight was on Saturday but I brought it forward by a day as my mother passed away a few days ago and my wife was having some health issues. I had planned to come back as soon as I could. I had told the Asian Hockey Federation that it would be my last tournament. I will consider legal action once I get back to Jalandhar, he said. Sangha, 54, hails from Jalandhar and has been officiating matches at the international level for more than a decade. Last year, he had faced a similar complaint from an Indian woman umpire during the 2024-2025 Hockey India League HIL. The complaint lodged with Hockey India at the time accused him of behaving with the umpire in a manner that was unprofessional, disrespectful, which created an extremely uncomfortable atmosphere for her on 20th January 2025, at approximately 4.20-4.25 pm in the lobby area of a hotel in Ranchi. Following the complaint, Sangha was removed from his officiating duties at the tournament, the Hockey India official said. Hockey India also set up a committee to probe the complaint but its findings were not made public, and Sangha went on to officiate in the mens Junior World Cup in Chennai and Madurai last year.

articleTitle: Suryakumar Yadav asked to confirm availability for Ranji Trophy, and then snubbed; Yashasvi Jaiswal picked
articleFeaturedImageAlt: FILE: Suryakumar Yadav in action. (CREIMAS for BCCI)
description: While Jaiswal found a place in the squad, Suryakumar was overlooked for the match scheduled from October 11 to 15.

articleTitle: ‘16 years apart’: Telangana High Court grants man divorce over false criminal case, cruelty
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Telangana High Court divorce false case cruelty The bench also noted that the wife’s allegations of dowry harassment and possession of her jewellery were “vague or unsupported”.
description: The wife had approached the women’s protection cell and lodged a criminal complaint over cruelty and dowry demands, following which the husband filed the divorce petition.
body_raw: The Telangana High Court has granted divorce to a couple after 16 years of separation, holding that a false criminal complaint against the husband and his family, coupled with prolonged separation, amounted to mental cruelty. The court set aside the family courts earlier dismissal of his petition. Dealing with a plea of husband, a bench of Justices K Lakshman and B R Madhusudhan Raosaid that the conduct of the parties clearly indicates that there is no intention on either side to lead a marital life. It is apt to note that when the petition was filed, the appellant was 33 years old and the respondent was 27 years old. At present, they are 49 years old and 42 years old, respectively. They have been living separately for approximately 16 years. The appellant has categorically stated that he is not willing to resume cohabitation or take her back into his society, the September 18 order reads. The bench further noted that the couple had been living separately for around 16 years, neither had made a genuine effort to resume living together, and the husband had clearly stated that he was unwilling to take the wife back. The court held that continuation of the marriage would serve no meaningful purpose and would cause mental cruelty to both parties. Husband sought divorce over cruelty The petitioner-husband has filed a plea challenging the 2017 order of the family court which dismissed his petition seeking divorce on grounds of cruelty. The couple got married in 2007. The husband sought divorce, claiming that after three to four months of marriage, the wife started harassing and torturing him, and insisted that he should become a puppet husband. He stated that she stopped performing her matrimonial obligations. The petitioner alleged that when he refused to accede to her demands, she physically assaulted him. He further alleged that her parents assured him that they would counsel her and took her away for around 10 days, but when she returned, she resumed abusing and harassing him. According to the husband, the two started living separately in the same house in separate rooms from 2008. He claimed that in 2009, she left the matrimonial home and started residing at her parental home. The wife denied the allegations and, in turn, accused the husband and his family of harassment, physical abuse, and interference in their marital life. She alleged that her mother-in-law and other family members subjected her to harassment and that the husband had also physically assaulted her. The matrimonial dispute escalated in 2010 after the wife and her father approached the womens protection cell, following which a criminal complaint was lodged against the husband and his family for cruelty and under the provisions of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The husband then filed the divorce petition in 2010, alleging cruelty. The family court initially dismissed the husbands divorce petition, holding that he had failed to establish cruelty through clear evidence. He challenged that decision before the high court. On the other hand, the criminal case against the husband and his family ended in acquittal in 2020, and the acquittal was upheld in 2025 following a plea. Wifes dowry claims unsupported Order The high court observed that cruelty is not defined by statute and whether a particular act amounts to cruelty depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. It said the court must consider the parties background, social and economic circumstances, values and the overall conduct between them. The ruling stressed that the cumulative effect of the parties conduct has to be considered rather than examining individual incidents in isolation. Persistent quarrels, humiliating treatment, mental harassment, abusive language, disrespectful behaviour, unilateral desertion and false accusations may constitute cruelty, while ordinary disagreements or petty quarrels would not. The bench also noted that the wifes allegations of dowry harassment and possession of her jewellery were vague or unsupported. The dowry allegation was raised for the first time during cross-examination, without details of any specific demand, while her claim regarding jewellery was found inconsistent with her own statement about having the keys to her almirah. The court held that the criminal complaint lodged by the wife against the husband and his family, which ended in acquittal and was also upheld in appeal, could be considered as subsequent evidence of cruelty. It is a well-settled legal position that when a criminal case ends in acquittal, it can be considered as a ground for cruelty, it concluded. The court clarified that subsequent events and the conduct of parties can be considered while examining a claim of cruelty. In this case, although the husbands own testimony was alone not enough to establish cruelty, the later acquittal in the criminal case, coupled with the wifes contradictory statements, supported his case.

articleTitle: India prevail in hockey, Pakistan triumph in volleyball, but handshakes win the day
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hockey players from India and Pakistan hug each other after their Asian Games semifinal match. (PTI)
description: A different picture of the cross-border rivalry was on display in sports not named cricket
body_raw: The scoreboard still read 25-18, the final point of Pakistans 3-0 win over India. But as Amit Balwan Singh stood talking about the defeat, Pakistans middle blocker Musaweer Khan ruffled his hair, Murad Khan consoled him and Abu Bakar Siddique walked over and patted him on the back. The Indian players are like my brothers, Siddique said. It was a gentle end to a match Pakistan had dominated, on a day that offered two different India-Pakistan results across two sports. In the morning, Pakistan beat India 3-0 in volleyball. In the evening, India beat Pakistan 4-3 in hockey - a semifinal that provided a glimpse of what the rivalry between the two could still produce, with players high-fiving each other before the push-back and captains shaking hands at the start. The two countries will meet again on Saturday, this time for the Asian Games cricket gold medal. There, the customary handshake has been absent in recent meetings, offering a different picture of the rivalry. Asked in the context of the cricket teams decision not to shake hands, Amit, an outside-hitter, said People look at India-Pakistan from a different point of view. But a sportsperson has to think about his best performance. The relations between the two countries havent been good since the beginning but a sportsperson has to ignore all that and focus on the game. Click here to read our Asian Games full coverage The volleyball court offered a glimpse of what he meant. Before the quarterfinal match, the teams exchanged pins and greeted each other. Once the whistle went, however, the familiarity gave way to the contest, with Pakistan attacking more cleanly and repeatedly finding ways around Indias block. Pakistan took the first set 25-19, fought back from 16-13 down to take the second 25-23 and then pulled away early in the third to win 25-18. The intensity was obvious during the match. Pakistan celebrated almost every point loudly, especially as India began to struggle in the third set. But the mood changed quickly once the contest ended. We were relaxed throughout, Siddique said, as Pakistan recorded a third straight win over India at the Asian Games. At 19, Siddique is one of the younger players in the Pakistan team. Sharing the athletes accommodation with the Indian side, he said, had given him a chance to learn from players he had previously known mainly as opponents. We are staying at the same hotel. I am a junior, so I learn a lot just by watching how they conduct themselves. What they eat, what they do, how they kit up. It feels very good to share space with seniors. We all eat together at the mess, he said. Siddique also spoke about Indian players with the familiarity of someone discussing teammates rather than rivals. Mashallah, all Indian players are good. I have seen Chirag Yadav, an outside-hitter a lot, theres Muthuswamy Appavu, a setter. Mashallah, he is also good. At CAVA Nations League, last year when India had won, he was very good, outstanding. I saw him and wondered, yeh kya kar raha hai what is he doing There is, of course, an awareness among the players of what an India-Pakistan fixture represents beyond the court. Abu Bakar said the hype surrounding the matches was largely a product of the rivalry built around them. Of course, there is hype when India and Pakistan play. But thats because of the way this rivalry has been turned into animosity. So thats what stays with us, India-Pakistan, India-Pakistan. But trust me, our two teams have a very good relationship, gupshup karte hai we do have chats, he said. There is familiarity and respect also because the players face each other in club colours. Indian and Pakistani spikers often ply their trade in volleyball leagues in central Asia. And, sharing a neutral ground has helped players understand each other better. I know Amit because we played two years ago together in Kazakhstan, said Khan, who hails from Pakistans volleyball-crazy district of Bannu, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. What happens outside sport does not reflect on our relationship when we play. Amit, who has played alongside Pakistani players at clubs in Iran, made the same distinction. This is, of course, a very important match. As a sportsperson, if we look at this match from that point of view, there will be more pressure. We can execute our skills if we play with a free mind. Out of the court, we speak to each other cordially. Sometimes, we end up playing for the same clubs abroad, like in Iran, he said. A few hours later, the result was reversed on the hockey field, but the drama was turned up several notches. India raced to a 3-0 lead, only for Pakistan to fight back and level the match at 3-3. With 49.2 seconds left, forward Abhishek Nains shot took a deflection off Sufiyan Khans stick and found the net for a thrilling 4-3 win and sent India into Saturdays final, where they will face Malaysia. When the match ended, the players, exhausted and overcome by emotion, shook hands before leaving the field. The hockey and volleyball players were not alone. Earlier in the Games, the India and Pakistan table tennis players, too, greeted each other warmly, as did their squash players. On Thursday, even as the results went one way in the morning and the other in the evening, the warmth stayed the same.

articleTitle: Munich Security Conference CEO Benedikt Franke: ‘India has said right things for years… not often lent its weight… It’s finally walking the talk’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: ‘India has said right things for years… not often lent its weight… It’s finally walking the talk’
description: “It’s okay to buy Russian oil, but I wish when you go into the shop, you don’t kiss the shopkeeper,” says Franke, as he welcomes India’s proposals on Russia-Ukraine war, hopes Delhi can use its “special relationship” with Moscow to end stalemate.
body_raw: India is ready to put its diplomatic weight and relationship into efforts to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end, says Benedikt Franke, Vice-Chairman and CEO of the Munich Security Conference MSC. In an expansive interview with The Indian Express, Franke, who is in Delhi for the Munich leaders meeting a chapter of the MSF held in different locations every year, spoke about the war and Indias active role in trying to resolve the conflict, Indias import of Russian energy, the US-Iran conflict, as well as the rise of the far right party AfD in Germany. Excerpts India has moved a proposal to end the war in Ukraine, going beyond advocating for dialogue and diplomacy. How do you see this? Im absolutely thrilled that India is finally walking the talk. Prime Minister Modi has said the right things for a while on this issue, that there is a need for dialogue, for negotiations. However, India didnt vote accordingly in the UN. Now, not just the Ukrainian foreign minister but also President Putin have has said that the proposals received from the Indian side were the only ones he was seriously considering. I hope more countries take note of this development. We Europe believe that our best hope lies with countries like India and China that have a special relationship with Russia. These countries are now finally ready to use their diplomatic weight and their relationship to support efforts to bring this war to an end. We hope it doesnt lead to a situation in which the aggressor Russia is rewarded and the victim Ukraine is punished. We, Europeans, will do everything we can to ensure that the Ukrainians end up in the strongest possible negotiation position. I just hope India sort of doubles down on these very promising signs. Why do you think the needle has moved for India? The Ukraine-Russia war comes at a cost for everyone. Countries like India need stability and predictability in global trade and relations. India needs to continue on its growth trajectory, to pull hundreds of millions out of poverty. Another reason is that multi-alignment is great on paper. It also comes to a natural limit at some point. Civilians are dying every day in Ukraine, civilian infrastructure is destroyed. How can you be a liberal democracy, position yourself as a leader in this world on inter-State cooperation, on development, and not act on blatant breaches of international law? And then, India is becoming more ambitious in a lot of fields, putting stuff in space, being an economic or technological powerhouse. But, on the diplomatic front, I dont think Indias actions to date matched its self-perception. Critics in Europe and the West say India is still buying Russian energy. India argues that it is acting in self-interest. Its perfectly okay to buy Russian oil and gas, but I wish that when you go into the shop to buy it, you dont kiss the shopkeeper. Why do we need selfies at the BRICS summit? Why do we need the embrace between Modi and Putin? Maybe we are underestimating the close emotional ties between India and Russia. We just hope that this special relationship can be, in a way, used to end the stalemate we are seeing. And by putting a little pressure on its favourite shopkeeper, India could make a major difference in the war. What do you make of US President Donald Trumps efforts for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war? I have been criticised in the past for praising President Trump for trying. I think trying is better than not trying, and I wish there were a European-led effort, but there is not. And so, everyone that tries to solve this without throwing the Ukrainians in front of the bus deserves praise. I am not 100 sure that President Trumps efforts and the focus on or connection to business interests of the United States in Russian resources was very helpful. It is perfectly okay for the United States to do business with Russia. At some point, I hope the European Union and India will do more business with Russia. At the end of the day, we want a stable, prosperous and constructive Russia. No one wants a tumbling giant like Russia. But first, it is based on an expectation that this war comes to an end, that aggression ends, that the sovereign territory of Ukraine is restored. If we have no agreement on that, having an agreement on business sends the wrong signal. But I could imagine that if you Indians broke the ice now, the US joining such an effort would make a huge difference. Is it still a stalemate after four-and a-half-years of the Ukraine war, and what does it mean for European security? For Ukraine, to be perfectly honest, its quite a success that they are still there. Europe has not done enough to help Ukraine win. Hence, it has not won. But we have done a lot to help them survive, get their house in order, and become a leader in defence technology. They are now producing most of the stuff they need themselves. We need to appreciate that this country, which is only a quarter of the population of Russia and only a fraction of its economic potential, has held out for four years. I dont want to paint a rosy picture. The winter will be terrible. The Russians have destroyed so much energy and other infrastructure. But they the Ukrainians are still there on a lot of sovereign territory, and here and there, they actually win battles, produce what we call iconoclastic victories and deep strikes into Russian territory. They, by the way, never attack civilian infrastructure. Now the question is, will Europe step up its effort to bring Ukraine into a good negotiating position? Will the US realise once again who the actual aggressor is? Will India and other powerhouses put a little pressure on Putin? I have no answer. How do you see the energy security issue playing out given the war in West Asia, on top of the Russia-Ukraine conflict? I am quite pessimistic that without a larger alliance of countries working, this conflict will be solved any time soon. I do not believe in some American predictions. I do not believe in the miraculous disappearance of the Houthis. I do not believe in a sudden end to Iranian ambitions. I wish for a stronger European role, a stronger American role, and a stronger Asian role in finding a diplomatic solution. I fear there is an implicit assumption of a division of labour globally in these conflicts. Europeans believe that is American-caused and it needs to be American-solved. Americans believe that Ukraine is Europes problem. If we continue this silo thinking. I dont think we will see a solution. The Iran conflict is also driving up prices in Germany at a time when our domestic politics are in a difficult place, when our industry is in a difficult place. That increases the chances of the right or the left fringes of the political spectrum to win. Do you think the rise of the right and the extreme right is here to stay, especially in Germany? As long as the political centre doesnt find clear answers to some of the worries that the population in Germany, but also across the world, has-personal security, job prospects, prosperity for their kids, crime, migration, culture-and enters into a national debate on these, the political extremes will be further empowered. Global governance, global multilateralism, will not be revitalised. How many Indians believe that the UN is their best chance? How many Indians put real faith into the World Bank and the IMF?. Take their worries, justified or not, seriously, and provide real, value-added solutions. If we dont, the extreme ends will win, and whether its left or right really makes no difference. In Germany, the extreme left is pretty close to the extreme right. Germany has a very close relationship with China, and the recent meeting between US President Trump and President Xi Jinping indicates some kind of rapprochement. The two superpowers need to de-escalate, need to clear the air occasionally. Hence it is to be welcomed. Its perfectly okay to be friends with China and the US at the same time, as it is perfectly okay for India to try to be friends with everyone at the same time. I mean, if multi-alignment works for you, why shouldnt it work for us? There is still an issue with human rights. But, at the end of the day, we want a strong, prosperous China that engages constructively in international relations. You have been coming to India for at least a decade now. How do you see Indias perception about itself, and its perception from where you sit in Germany? I love coming to this country because the feeling of dynamism, of optimism, is just infectious and great. Indian interlocutors have become more confident. They see their economic growth rate. They see the many Indian success stories, the space programme.. But With superpower status come responsibilities. At some point, multi-alignment will come to a natural limit. You will have to choose sides on certain issues at some point. India has said the right things for many years. It hasnt necessarily put its full weight behind these statements.

articleTitle: Safari season is back: What to know before visiting India’s national parks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: First-time safari-goers should look beyond tiger sightings and observe the wider forest ecosystem in National Parks.
description: As India’s national parks reopen after the monsoon, experts share what first-time safari-goers should know before heading into the forest.
body_raw: Monsoon is when our forests breathe without disturbance. However, after being closed or operating with restrictions during the rainy months, several national parks and wildlife sanctuaries are now reopening for visitors. From Ranthambore and Sariska Tiger Reserves in Rajasthan to Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand and other wildlife destinations, the reopening marks the return of the safari season in several parts of the country. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Talking about Jim Corbett, Ajay Kareer, general manager, Corbett Hideaway, Jim Corbett - IHCL SeleQtions says, Every reopening of Corbett after the monsoon brings a renewed sense of anticipation for wildlife enthusiasts. The forest is dense and green, the Kosi is flowing at its fullest, and there is movement everywhere, from birds and butterflies to elephants and deer emerging into the open. Know these before heading for your first safari For those heading out on their first safari, the anticipation of a tiger sighting is naturally a major part of the excitement. However, experts say that visitors should approach a safari with a broader understanding of the forest and the inhabitants. Renuka Natu, Founder of Africa with Renuka, and Kareer share certain things travellers should keep in mind Tread carefully as you re-enter wild spaces. Take a moment to soak in all that the backdrop has to offer the birds, the bees, the butterflies the wasps the bears the antelope the elephants and the tigers. Visitors should look beyond just the tiger and notice the many signs of a thriving ecosystem. An alarm call, a herd moving through the grass or a fresh pugmark can turn an ordinary stretch of forest into a moment of discovery. Take note of the necessary guidelines and respect animals space, rather than expecting every safari to deliver a particular sighting. The most memorable safaris are often those where you slow down, observe and allow the forest to reveal itself in all its song and glory. articleTitle: Heart of the Beast movie review: Brad Pitt powers a gripping, deeply moving survival drama
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Brad Pitt movie Heart of the Beast review
description: Heart of the Beast review: Much of what makes David Ayer's Heart of the Beast gripping and deeply moving is down to Brad Pitt.
body_raw: Heart of the Beast movie review A man and his dog walk across 58 miles of Alaskan wilderness, fighting a heart attack, plane crash, injury, bears, wolves, drowning. David Ayer and Brad Pitt collaborate for the second time, after Fury, for this unlikely film about a bond between a retired US Special Forces Sergeant Major and his combat scout dog. A bond that has been forged during one of those indistinguishable and bloody tours of duty that America keeps rushing into. The PTSD that follows afflicts not just James Pitt but also Odin, and the two are spending time now in a part of Alaska that is even more isolated than the rest of it. They have no company but each other - barring a visit by a mysterious retired gold miner played gamely by Simmons. And beyond their two trunks of essentials carrying everything from medicines and maps to food and clothes, and a belt with pouches carrying more of the same tied around Odin, they dont need anyone else. However, the peaceful escape of James and Odin into the quiet of nature - broken only faintly by the swish of wind, the call of birds, the rustle of rushing water in a stream, or that dripping off leaves after a bout of rain - ends abruptly. What follows is the walk, to find help, with Jamess body put through the kind of injuries and pain that would kill any mortal who doesnt have a dog like Odin by their side, or the training of a US Special Forces soldier, or a camping kit of a well-prepared American. That Heart of the Beast is as gripping as it is, and deeply moving, is due to Pitt. The star with his undeniable charm has embraced his age, and both the length of those years and the depth of his time spent with Odin - and the strength he derives from this - are etched on his face and reflect in his eyes. Odin, played by four different German Shepherds, is in sync with Jamess every mood and movement, his eyes constantly searching, weighing. But for unnecessary flashbacks to whatever war James and Odin were in last, leaving Odin with an amputated leg, Ayer doesnt deviate from their story. Or from Alaska. The perils of this path are entirely common, nothing dramatic about them or anything particularly heroic in how James and Odin survive. The tussle with the wolves, though, may leave you with nightmares. Eventually, the film does have one too many perils. A few near rescues or some more quieter flashback moments may have helped give a break. Heart of the Beast movie director David Ayer Heart of the Beast movie cast Brad Pitt, J K Simmons Heart of the Beast movie rating 3.5 stars

articleTitle: In every trans woman’s life, there is a Dorothy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: In every trans woman’s life, there is a Dorothy
description: To shift the collective consciousness and urge the public to view every person as human, Tamil cinema needs hundreds of more films like Dorothy, Super Deluxe, and Natchathiram Nagargiradhu
body_raw: A society disturbed by a kiss must first ask why it is unable to see a trans womans pain, love, and humanity. The Tamil film Dorothy, directed by Karthik Subbaraj, engages with a society still struggling to recognise transgender people as complete human beings. What troubles us is not the debate surrounding the film, but what this has chosen to focus on. A story exploring caste, patriarchy, family, systemic violence, toxic masculinity, and gender politics has been reduced to one question How can a trans woman kiss a man? Why does that kiss spark such moral panic? Calling it two men kissing reveals a refusal to recognise a trans woman as a woman. But beyond that, why should intimacy cause such discomfort? Set in the 1990s, Dorothy reminds us of the real-life Dorothys whose stories were never documented, living through an era where gender, caste, and class inflicted severe violence on womens bodies. Through a sharp intergenerational lens, Subbaraj confronts a centuries-old system now struggling to digest the truth. This conflict forces a deeper inquiry into identity Who is Dorothy to Subbu? Is she a mother? A sister? A sister-in-law? Before demanding answers, society must face a simpler question Do you accept Subbu as Dorothy? Change is not an overnight process, but opposing and ignoring the struggles of another human remains deeply inhumane. A section of viewers forgets how Subbu struggled to guard her kaitiakitanga, her protective, nurturing femininity in a male-dominated world, only to obsess over a single kiss in the final scene. In truth, Dorothy represents the collective feminine that nurtures and protects a trans womans emerging identity. In real life, Dorothy takes many forms Mothers, mentors, female educators. In every trans womans life, there is a Dorothy most often, she is another woman. Music is a vital pillar of this sanctuary. For decades, mainstream Tamil cinema offered transgender and queer people little more than ridicule. In Dorothy, Ilaiyaraajas score feels like a balm to those wounds. Music provides a space where trans women safely explore their identity, historically through Ilaiyaraaja and Swarnalatha compositions like Enulle enulle, and Muthumani, now a trans anthem. In many ways, Ilaiyaraaja himself embodies Dorothy through the emotional shelter his art bestows. The films visual grammar speaks volumes. Karthiks choices such as the slow-motion parotta and salna sequence or the sharp presence of the chappathi kalli prickly pear cactus vividly convey the weight of toxic masculinity enforced upon trans bodies. This depth extends to performance and casting. Sanaths performance deserves appreciation for its vulnerability and commitment. Yet, when cisgender actors consistently receive accolades for portraying transgender characters, it raises an undeniable question Where does that leave trans actors who have spent years fighting simply to be cast? At the same time, Dorothys inclusion of trans actors and the international platform given to artists like Jeeva is meaningful. True representation must extend beyond who plays the lead it must be about who gets access to opportunities. Dorothy is a gift and a necessary step forward. To shift the collective consciousness and urge the public to view every person as human, Tamil cinema needs hundreds of more films like Dorothy, Super Deluxe, and Natchathiram Nagargiradhu. Negha is an actor, writer, and co-founder of Queer Casting, Angamuththu is a law student
